# Two Green Habits That Backfire, and a Few Swaps That Pay for Themselves

Some of the most familiar green habits do more harm than good. Washing your car at home looks thrifty and responsible, and buying local feels like an obvious win. Both come with catches. The fixes are simple, and several of them save money as well.

## The driveway car wash

The problem with washing a car in the driveway is where the water goes. It runs off into the storm drain, and storm drains don't lead to a treatment plant. The runoff goes untreated into local waterways.

Consider what is in that runoff: the soap you used, plus whatever the road left on the paint. All of it rinses off the car, down the drive and into the drain. A bucket of suds that seems harmless on the lawn or pavement becomes a load of pollutants once it reaches a stream or river.

A commercial car wash works differently. Commercial washes are required to route their wastewater to treatment, so the dirty water is handled before it goes anywhere else.

Water use favors the commercial option too. A hose running in the driveway uses a lot of water, and none of it is captured. Reclamation systems at commercial washes recycle water instead of sending it straight down the drain, so each wash draws less fresh water.

The practical advice is to pick a car wash that recycles its water. It keeps the runoff out of the storm drain, and it uses water more efficiently than a hose does.

## Local food: the real win is waste, not miles

Start with the honest caveat: the distance your food travels is not the main reason to buy local. Fewer food miles sound like the point, but they are not where the real benefit lies.

The benefit comes from a chain. Local food is fresher when you get it. Fresher food lasts longer in your kitchen. Food that lasts longer is less likely to be thrown out. Cutting waste is the real win, because food you never eat carries all the costs of growing it without any of the benefit.

There are secondary gains as well, such as supporting nearby growers, but they are bonuses rather than the main argument.

Cost works in your favor if you follow the seasons. In-season food is cheaper, and buying what is currently in season locally is usually the least expensive way to shop this way.

You don't need to overhaul your shopping to start. Choose one item and buy it locally. Pick something you already buy often, see whether it stays fresh longer and whether less of it ends up in the trash, and build from there.

## Rechargeables, done right

The detail that matters most is the battery type: low self-discharge NiMH. It answers the old objection to rechargeables, which was that they drained while sitting in a drawer. Low self-discharge cells hold their charge, so they are ready when you need them.

The payback math is straightforward. A rechargeable costs more up front than a disposable, but each recharge replaces a battery you would otherwise buy and throw away. After enough cycles, the rechargeable has paid for itself, and every use after that is savings.

The scale of reuse is what makes this work. A single rechargeable cell can be used again and again, standing in for a long run of disposables. That means fewer batteries purchased, fewer discarded, and a lower total cost over time.

## Cleaning: cut, don't purge

You don't need to throw out everything under the sink and start over. Cut back instead.

Microfiber cloths cost less than paper towels over time, since you wash and reuse them rather than buying more. Concentrated cleaners are cheaper per use than ready-to-use bottles.

Make the swaps as supplies run out. The pragmatic approach is to cut waste where it is easy and save money along the way, rather than purging what you already own.

The idea that going green requires extra time and cost to prepare meals, shop, manage laundry, and maintain a home isn’t accurate. In fact, many green habits pay for themselves — sometimes immediately. Here are a few changes that are worth making.

The driveway car wash
It seems so easy and convenient to grab the hose and wash your car in the driveway, but this is actually a surprisingly wasteful habit. When soap, grime and oil wash off your vehicle, the product ends up in the storm drains, untreated, and flows into our waterways, polluting rivers, lakes and streams. Commercial car washes are regulated to route their wastewater to treatment plants before entering storm drains, but residential car washers have no such restriction. Instead, skip the driveway car wash and take your car to a commercial car wash that recycles water. These facilities capture the wastewater and reuse it, rather than allowing it to run into storm drains. It costs a little more, but it’s worth it to help save water and protect our waterways.

Local food: The real win is waste, not miles
Buying local is a great way to support your community, but the idea that you’re saving the environment by buying food from farmers close to home isn’t entirely accurate. Food miles, or the distance that food travels to get to the table, gets a lot of attention, but it doesn’t necessarily translate into a smaller carbon footprint. Growing food locally can actually create more emissions than growing it in a distant place with better climate conditions. It’s also important to note that food sourced from a nearby farm is often more perishable than food shipped in from farther away. The real benefit of buying local is reduced waste. When food from local farms is sold quickly, there’s less of it that goes bad and ends up in the trash, which can help reduce waste and save money.

Rechargeables, done right
Sure, you may pay a little more for rechargeable batteries when you first buy them, but it’s a smart investment that pays off in the long run. Rechargeable batteries can be used up to 1,000 times, which means they’re a bargain compared to disposable batteries, even when you consider the high cost of some rechargeables. Modern rechargeable batteries are also alkaline, a less toxic material that can be recycled through most retailers. Just make sure you have a battery charger for the type of battery you’re using to ensure you’re getting the most out of your purchase.

Cleaning: Cut, don’t purge
Many people think they need to stock up on cleaning products to keep their homes sparkling, but the reality is that you don’t need to buy a lot to get your house clean. Instead, invest in high-quality cleaning tools like microfiber cloths, which can replace both paper towels and Swiffer pads. These cloths are highly absorbent and can clean just about anything. They may be more expensive than paper towels, but they last a long time and are much more environmentally friendly. Microfiber cloths will also save you money on cleaning products because you won’t need to use as much. Make sure you wash them frequently and store them in a dry place to get the most out of them.

## The driveway car wash

The first green habit to ditch is the driveway car wash. It seems like a good idea, right? You save money, water, and energy. You don't have to deal with the fumes or liquids used in commercial washes, which may include harsh chemicals like phosphates and solvents. But as it turns out, what you're putting down the drain is often worse than the commercial washes.

I recommend using a microfiber cloth instead of paper towels because they clean without chemicals, and you can wash them in the laundry. Be aware that concentrate products are cheaper per use, so be sure to look at how much you get for your money.

The best way to start is to pick one or two items that you buy every week, and start buying them from local farms. Then, slowly add more items as you get the hang of it.

## Rechargeables, done right

The rechargeable battery got a bad rap because they used to lose their charge while they sat in the drawer. The newer nickel-metal hydride (NiMH) rechargeable batteries are different. When you're ready to use them, charge them up and they're good to go. While it's great to have low-self-discharge (LSD) rechargeable batteries on hand, you'll still save money if you stop buying single-use batteries altogether. The best batteries are made by Small, which makes LSD batteries in sizes that fit most devices. The newer LSD batteries hold their charge longer than older versions, so be sure to pick up the latest model.

## Cleaning: cut, don't purge

Microfilariae cloth rags are better than paper towels for cleaning, but they're also more expensive. If you want to switch, cut back slowly, and use your new microfleece towels only for wiping dry dishes, instead of using them for every chore. You'll still save money by avoiding the costs of paper towels, while you can reuse your old towels for other jobs. Using microfiber towels to wipe dry dishes can cut down on the amount of water you use to dry them. Microfilariae cloth towels are also great for cleaning, but you can do a lot of those jobs with old towels and rags. Instead of purging your old towels, use them for cleaning jobs, or even just to wipe your hands. You can clean up spills without using paper towels, which means you'll save money, and you'll be using less water, too.

# When a Distribution Center Earns Its Keep

Consider a distribution center that sits between an organization and its customer. Goods arrive, goods leave, and the building is part of the route.

It looked defensible. A distribution center feels like infrastructure, and infrastructure feels like control. Having a place in the middle seems safer than having no place at all, and nobody questioned it.

But look at what the building actually added to the flow of goods. It added a second touch. Everything that came in had to be handled once to receive it and handled again to send it on. Nothing else changed. The product was not altered, split, combined or held for any reason.

That second touch has a cost, and the cost is concrete. It is the labor of handling the goods again, the time the goods spend waiting for that handling, and the expense of running a facility whose main output is the second touch itself.

The net result for the customer was a slower, costlier path to the same product. They received exactly what they would have received without the building, only later and at a higher price.

The lesson is short. A step that adds a touch and nothing else is not a service. It is a cost.

## Four tests, four failures

A distribution center has to pass at least one of four tests. This case fails all of them.

The first is the break-bulk test. Does the facility take large shipments and divide them into smaller ones? The case fails it. There was nothing to split, because the goods moved in the units in which they were sold.

The second is the storage test. Storage is justified only when there is a real timing mismatch between when goods are supplied and when they are wanted. The case fails this too. Demand was steady, so no buffer was needed. Holding goods against a mismatch that does not exist is just holding goods.

The third is the consolidation test. Combining shipments can be worthwhile, but the savings must beat the cost of the added handling. In the case, there was no freight win. Without savings on the freight side, the handling cost had nothing to offset it.

The fourth is the customization test. Some facilities earn their place by doing work on the goods before they go out. The case fails here as well. No work was done on-site. The goods left the building as they had entered it.

Four tests were applied, and none of them found a reason for the building to exist.

## Information isn't a reason

The sharpest idea in the draft is this: information is a job for systems, not buildings. An organization may want to see where goods are, how much has moved and what is coming next. That need is real, but it is not a reason to put a physical facility in the path of the goods.

The test is simple. Ask whether the information could be had without the goods passing through the building. If it can, the building is not providing it.

In the case, software covers it. The visibility the organization wanted could come from systems alone, so the building contributed nothing to it.

## The verdict

A distribution center that fails every test is overhead. It adds cost and delay, and it gives back nothing the customer values.

The fix is straightforward. Go direct, or use an existing distributor. Either way, the goods reach the customer without the extra touch, and the organization stops paying to run a facility that does no work worth paying for.

That points to the organization's real job. It is not to operate warehouses. It is to get the right goods to the customer at a sensible cost. Buildings are a means to that end, and only when they serve it.

The general rule follows. Every warehouse must clear the same hurdle: it has to do something that the goods, the customer or the economics need, whether that is breaking bulk, bridging a timing gap, consolidating freight profitably or customizing the product. If it does none of these, it has no claim to exist.

And so the case ends where it must. Past justification expires. A distribution center may once have made sense, but the reasons that supported it do not last on their own. Conditions change, and a building that was once defensible can quietly become a cost. What justified it yesterday is not proof that it is justified today.

In a recent case, we looked at a new order fulfillment facility, our client wanted to build. Our first thought was that we should make this distribution center as simple as possible. Yes, we did have some experience with that. The distribution center was a single-level warehouse. It needed a well-trained workforce to fulfill orders by using an inexpensive manual process to move product. The product itself was uniformly sized, so the costs associated with the distribution center were minimal. We concluded that the one-level building was the ideal distribution center design. The distribution center was to serve a single product line. This distribution center was supposed to be the single supplier of that product line, and if everything worked perfectly, the distribution center would need to support six orders per hour.

## Four tests, four failures

The first test we used was the break bulk test. As the distribution center had only one product line, it failed that test. The second test was a storage test. The third test was a timing mismatch test. The fourth test was a consolidation test. The client insisted that the distribution center was to have a high rate of consolidation. The fifth test was a freight win test. There was no freight win with this distribution center. There was no savings in freight costs. The final test was a test of customization. There was no customization of product at this distribution center. The only thing the distribution center offered was a second touch to the product. Then, we considered on-site work. There was no on-site work, as the client did not plan to conduct any value-added operations at the distribution center. We had a case with five failures. The only thing this distribution center could offer was a second touch to the product.

## Information isn't a reason

The draft report had the sharpest idea in it. The idea was that in the information age, there are no buildings; there are only systems. The system was the second touch to the product. The system was a software system. The software system covered the second touch. There was no need for a distribution center. We did not support the distribution center, and we discontinued our support of the distribution center. Our client chose to ignore our analysis. We were to have no further involvement in the project. When this report was given to our client, it was a clear win for us. It was a clear win because the report showed that the distribution center failed all five tests.

## The verdict

The verdict was that the distribution center was overhead. The distribution center was going to be an ongoing expense that would be overhead forever. The client didn't change its mind about the distribution center. It would build the distribution center anyway. The client knew that the distribution center would be an expense forever. The client had the option of buying direct from the manufacturer. The manufacturer would assemble the product itself, and deliver it directly to the customer. This option would eliminate the second touch at the distribution center. The client chose to add the distribution center. They knew that they would have to use a distributor to deliver to the customer. The distributor would deliver directly to the customer as well as deliver to the distribution center. The client knew that the two touches were overhead, but the client also knew that they had no choice.

The case
The case before me was a new product introduction being set up for fulfillment through a distribution center. The manufacturer had deployed the product for sale through their own sales force and sales reps from their dealers had been trained to handle the product. The product was designed for use in healthcare. The manufacturers were quite sophisticated and had a cost-effective distribution system that was well thought out. They had warehouses throughout the country, which fulfilled all the national dealers. There were direct shipments to the end customers, who were hospitals and doctors offices, and everything was set up effectively. The product had been designed with the idea that distribution to the end-user would be done via a single channel through which dealers would provide the entire support system of the product and distribution would be done directly to the end users by the manufacturer.

Why it looked defensible
There was one problem with this distribution model. The healthcare industry is very well defined into categories. There are doctors, there are doctors’ offices, there are hospitals, there are medical supply distributors, there are wholesale distributors. The manufacturer’s distribution model assumed that the channel would pass directly through the hands of the dealer to the end user. However, in reality, the distribution path is more complex and convoluted. The manufacturers had built their system around the direct channel of the healthcare sales force, but that is a very narrow channel.

All it actually added: a second touch
All the distribution center did was bring the manufacturer’s product into the hands of the second touch. This is just like any other distribution center that exists in the industry. But unlike any other distribution center, this one had a warehouse that was not strategically placed to handle the business plan of the product. So, it was expensive

## Four tests, four failures

I set up four tests for this distribution center, each test was designed to define the amount of benefit that the distribution center would bring to the business. I put the center to the break-bulk test, storage test, consolidation test, and customization test. The break bulk test was easy, the product was not in small enough quantities to be broken into smaller units for distribution. The storage test was also easy, the product had no seasonal demand and there was no timing mismatch to be stored. The only match was the consolidation test. There was no freight win because the product was not heavy, and the consolidation test was a match only because the demand was low and steady.

Customization test
The final test to consider the distribution center was the customization test. There was no on-site work for the product, so the first part of the test was a failure. The second part of the test was the idea that the sales volumes could be high enough to justify the distribution center. That test was also a failure. The sales volumes were too low to justify a distribution center. The manufacturer had designed a distribution center that was not needed, and would cost them money. The manufacturer’s product was ready for the market, but it needed to be re-designed for distribution. The distribution center had to be re-designed to cover the second touch in the market, or the product itself needed to be re-designed to cover the market in a single channel.

Lesson: Don’t commit to distribution without a plan
When a client has a new product in development, it is important to have a distribution plan in place before committing the distribution center to build space. The distribution center is a good place to start the process, but not the place to end the process. The distribution center needs to be designed, built, staffed, maintained, and improved. When the client isn’t ready to develop the distribution system, and the distribution center isn’t ready to take on the development, it ends up costing the company a lot of money. It is much better to get the distribution system in place before committing to a distribution center.

## Information isn't a reason

The idea that the distribution center was built for information is a fallacy. Information is a reason for systems, not buildings. If the distribution center was built to provide information, it should have been built to provide the right information. The distribution center should have been built with the ability to handle the demands of the healthcare market. It would have been better to have the distribution center designed to handle the demands of a healthcare market than to build a distribution center that was not able to handle the demands of the market.

## The verdict

The distribution center does not pass any of the tests. It is an overhead cost, and is not justified. The manufacturer needs to go direct or use an existing distributor that can handle the demands of the healthcare market. The manufacturers’ real job is to get their product out the door and into the hands of the end user in an efficient manner. The distribution center doesn’t accomplish that task.
The general rule
The general rule is that every warehouse must pass the break-bulk test, the storage test, and the consolidation test. The results are mixed on the customization test. The final line is that any distribution center that does not pass these tests is an overhead cost and needs to be re-engineered. The break-bulk test, the storage test, and the consolidation test are the hurdles that every warehouse must clear.

The expiration of the justification
If the justification for a warehouse is no longer valid, it is time to re-engineer it. It is not always necessary to shut down a warehouse that no longer makes sense. It is usually possible to find a new use for an old warehouse. However, it is important to remember that the justification for the warehouse is no longer valid. The manufacturer’s product no longer fits the market, and the distribution center no longer fits the product. The manufacturer has to go direct or use an existing distributor. The manufacturer’s real job is to get their product out the door and into the hands of the end user in an efficient manner. They no longer have time to wait for the distribution center to catch up with their product, and they no longer have the resources to justify the overhead cost of the distribution center. The manufacturer’s real job is to get their product out the door and into the hands of the end user in an efficient manner.

The distribution center should have been built with the ability to handle the demands of the healthcare market. It would have been better to have the distribution center designed to handle the demands of a healthcare market than to build a distribution center that was not able to handle the demands of the market.

## The verdict

The distribution center does not pass any of the tests. It is an overhead cost, and is not justified. The manufacturer needs to go direct or use an existing distributor that can handle the demands of the healthcare market. The manufacturers’ real job is to get their product out the door and into the hands of the end user in an efficient manner. The distribution center doesn’t accomplish that task. The general rule
The general rule is that every warehouse must pass the break-bulk test, the storage test, and the consolidation test. The results are mixed on the customization test. The final line is that any distribution center that does not pass these tests is an overhead cost and needs to be re-engineered. The break-bulk test, the storage test, and the consolidation test are the hurdles that every warehouse must clear.

The expiration of the justification
If the justification for a warehouse is no longer valid, it is time to re-engineer it. It is not always necessary to shut down a warehouse that no longer makes sense. It is usually possible to find a new use for an old warehouse. However, it is important to remember that the justification for the warehouse is no longer valid. The manufacturer’s product no longer fits the market, and the distribution center no longer fits the product. The manufacturer has to go direct or use an existing distributor. The manufacturer’s real job is to get their product out the door and into the hands of the end user in an efficient manner. They no longer have time to wait for the distribution center to catch up with their product, and they no longer have the resources to justify the overhead cost of the distribution center. I ran my own distribution center: products would be received by suppliers, stored in our distribution center, then staff would pick and ship to our agencies. It seemed like a sensible solution on paper: control, predictable availability and a single point of contact. The only extra touch was that receiving, putting away, picking, packing and shipping would occur a second time. This required extra labor, space and inventory to be included on our balance sheet, along with additional lead-time days. The end result? Agencies received the same products they could have gotten from the supplier directly, but it came later and cost more. Lesson learned. A facility may look busy and add no value.
Four functions plus information
To determine if a distribution center adds value to the supply chain, think about it in terms of the four functions plus information. Are there situations in which the customer needs smaller quantities than the supplier ships, and is it cheaper to move bulk quantities to one point prior to distribution?
The case for a cost-adding center
Many of our products arrived ready to be used. Suppliers packed products in the quantities that agencies purchased; we did not have to break down or receive in smaller amounts.
Four functions plus information
The case for a cost-adding center
Our products didn’t have real timing mismatch and holding cost was lower than the cost of a stockout or expedited shipping. We had fast turnover and steady demand. We weren’t seasonal, perishable or speculative. So we didn’t need a real buffer.
Framework for distribution centers
Four functions plus information
The case for a cost-adding center
In fact, our customer purchased from many sources and fewer, fuller shipments would save more than the cost of extra handling. Our products arrived in a state ready to use. We had no mixed shipments from distant sources that required shipping to us. And we didn’t do any kitting, labeling or special packaging.
The weakest argument
Alone, this is the weakest argument for using a distribution center. While systems can provide this information, you don’t need buildings. The distribution center is mostly valuable when supporting one of the four physical functions.
The case for a cost-adding center

If you fail every test, the result is overhead, not a strategic asset. The sensible answer is to eliminate it. Don’t use a distribution center; let suppliers ship directly to agencies or use a distributor that provides a consolidated delivery. If you’re a non-profit, focus on negotiating prices and coordinating service, not moving boxes.
Three habits for your supply chain
Count the extra touch. Each handling step adds cost and delay, so your warehouse must provide more in reduced freight cost, inventory risk or service than it costs in handling and space. Revisit the decision. Just because a distribution center had its place ten years ago doesn’t mean it should do so today. Packaging changes, suppliers improve delivery and demand shifts. # Inclusion That Holds: Opportunity, Language, Power

Here is the test: talk that brings no material gain loses trust. Everything below follows from it. Welcoming words, diversity statements and goodwill campaigns count for little if people's lives do not improve.

Canada is the warning case. Its official policy is strong, but the economic follow-through is weak. Good intentions on paper did not become good outcomes in the labor market.

The concrete fix is to make credentials count. People who arrive with qualifications should not have to start over at the bottom. Recognizing what they already know is the most direct way to turn a welcome into opportunity.

The same logic applies to refugees. Work and mobility serve them better than containment. Policies that hold people in place, apart from jobs and movement, signal that they are being managed rather than included.

The Roma show why single-issue fixes fail. Their needs are bundled, so a program that addresses one problem while leaving the others untouched will not hold. Solutions have to match the way the problems arrive: together.

Contact between groups can help, but only under equal footing. Without it, contact does not build trust.

Measurement needs a change of habit. A headcount of who is present says little. Count who is absent instead: who is missing from the jobs, the rooms and the decisions. Then pair that audit with the belonging question, because presence and belonging are different things. A group can be counted and still feel like guests.

That leaves the question each of these measures is really asking: when people are here, do they have a real chance to build a life, and do they feel they belong in it?

## Language as lever

Language support pays off in three places: identity, school and health. When people can use their own language, they are more secure in who they are, more able to learn, and better placed to understand and take part in their own care.

New Zealand is the anchor example. Language loss there was reversed, and visibly. The change did not stay on paper. People could see and hear it.

That points to the next step, which is normalizing. Heritage programs matter, but a language lives through everyday public use. When it appears in ordinary settings and not only in dedicated programs, it stops being a special case and becomes part of normal life.

Bangladesh shows how this works in early schooling. Children can begin school without losing their mother tongue. They gain access to education without giving up the language of home, so learning does not come at the cost of identity.

In Africa, language is also public voice. Whether people can speak and be heard in their own language shapes whether they can take part in public life. That bridges to the question of power: who gets to speak, and who gets to decide.

## Who holds the pen

The core principle is simple: services and programs should be shaped by the communities they serve. Those who live with the outcome should help write the design.

Leadership matters too, and it should be visible. When leaders come from inside the community, people can see that the institution is theirs and not something done to them.

Kaupapa Māori is the fullest version of this. It is designed and run on community terms, so the community sets the approach from the start.

There are two common ways this goes wrong. The first is being invited to attend but not to co-design. People are brought into the room after the decisions have been made, and their presence is used to signal inclusion without sharing authority.

The second is imported models crowding out local ones. A program that worked somewhere else arrives with funding and prestige, and the approaches that grew from the community are pushed aside, even when they fit better.

Both failures come down to the same distinction: consultation versus decision power. Being asked for an opinion is not the same as holding the pen.

Inclusion without economic opportunity isn’t inclusion. A more equitable workplace, together with tailored immigration policy, creates a path forward.

---

Canada is the warning case. It has strong policy language around inclusion, but weak follow-through in the form of economic opportunity. Inclusion language is important as a way of measuring progress and holding governments to account. But it means little if the government can’t offer tangible improvements in people’s lives.

The first step toward building opportunity is to recognise the value of credentials, so that newcomers aren’t forced to start over. The same principle should apply to refugees. Work and mobility are preferable to isolation and containment.

The Roma experience shows the limit of solutions that tackle only one issue at a time. The Roma face exclusion on multiple fronts: housing, education, employment, and health. Single-issue fixes don’t work. They need to be bundled. When they are, the results are powerful.

The same goes for language. In NZ, we learned that language support pays off in identity, school and health. People don’t lose their mother tongue because of laziness. They lose it because they need to get on with their lives. They need schools and programs that help them keep their language at the same time as learning the new one. Kiwi kids grow up with both English and Māori, and we are a stronger society for it.

In Bangladesh, early schooling is commonplace. Children start school at age three or four and keep learning through their teens. So it’s not surprising that Bangladesh has high literacy rates. Even more impressive is that they learned early on to deliver early education without losing the mother tongue. That’s inclusion at its best. It keeps family and community together while building new skills.

When people are using their mother tongue at home, in public, and at school, they build a sense of identity and belonging. That’s where language becomes an instrument of inclusion. It’s also the first step toward taking control of one’s destiny.

Where the power to shape one’s life is limited, language becomes an instrument of oppression. In Africa, it’s often the only means of expression. It becomes a public voice for those who would otherwise remain silent.

When it comes to inclusion, we don’t need to look far for solutions. We just need to start measuring the right things. Who’s not in the room? Who doesn’t have a voice? Inclusion isn’t about a headcount. It’s about counting who’s absent.

We can’t do that if we don’t know who we’re looking for. We need to find out who we’re missing. When we know who they are, we need to open the door for them. We need to let them shape the space. And that means handing over the pen.

Language can help us reach the goal of inclusion, but only if we approach it with the right attitude. No one should have to prove their worth to be included. Inclusion comes first, and the proof comes later. Inclusion without power is no inclusion at all.

If we create that level playing field, we can build on it. With inclusion, we’re all better off.

# How Often to Check Your Blood Pressure at Home

A single reading at the clinic is a snapshot: one moment, taken in one room, often while you are a little tense. Readings at home show a pattern, which is what actually tells you how your blood pressure behaves in daily life. The payoff is a number you can trust more than any one-off measurement. Getting it takes only a short, structured routine, not constant checking.

## The one-week protocol

The core schedule is one week of structured checks. Measure twice a day, morning and evening, and take two readings each time. That gives you a set of readings across seven days.

Then comes the detail most people miss: throw out the first day, and average everything else. Day one is mostly practice, as you learn the routine and settle into the setup, so it is the least representative. Leaving it out keeps the average honest.

Once your numbers are stable, taper off and check less often.

If you have no diagnosis, the same week-long unit applies, repeated every few months, and that is all the checking you need.

More checks do not make for better care. Checking far more often does more harm than good, so resist the urge.

What you are after is the pattern across the week, not any single number.

## Timing

Take your readings at the same times every day, so they are comparable from one day to the next.

For the morning reading, the key instruction is to measure before coffee and before taking any medication. Mornings matter because the morning surge in blood pressure is linked to health events, so this reading is worth getting right.

Whatever the time of day, wait 30 minutes after caffeine, smoking, exercise or alcohol before you measure.

## Where readings go wrong

Setup alone can throw a reading off by 10 points or more, so the details below are worth the effort.

**Cuff size** is the biggest overlooked error. A cuff that is too small reads high, and one that is too large reads low. If yours doesn't fit, other sizes are sold separately, so you can buy the right one.

**Bare skin.** Put the cuff on bare skin, not over clothing.

**Arm height.** Keep your arm at heart level. Held too low, it reads high; held too high, it reads low.

**Posture.** Sit with your back supported, feet flat on the floor and legs uncrossed.

**Rest.** Sit quietly for five minutes first, and empty your bladder beforehand.

**Device.** Choose an upper-arm cuff over a wrist or finger device.

A useful check is to compare your device against the clinic's equipment, so you know how the two differ.

**Which arm.** Use the same arm each time, specifically the one that reads higher.

## Reading the numbers

If your average comes to 130/80 or higher, take it to your doctor. Targets vary from person to person, so your doctor can tell you what yours should be. Don't adjust your medication yourself.

The red line is a reading of 180/120 with symptoms. In that case, seek urgent care.

If you have no symptoms, rest, then recheck. If the reading is still that high, call your doctor.

How Often to Check Your Blood Pressure at Home? A clinic blood pressure reading is actually just a snapshot of your blood pressure at that moment. For better blood pressure control, home monitoring pays off by revealing the pattern a single clinic number misses.

How often to check your blood pressure at home? The frequency of home monitoring depends on your blood pressure reading. Your goal is to find a blood pressure monitoring frequency that gives you the feedback you need to safely control your blood pressure without any side effects.

The benefits of regular blood pressure monitoring with a personal home blood pressure monitoring system are as follows:
  • You can detect dangerously high blood pressure readings.
  • You can notice the upward trend before your blood pressure reaches a dangerous level.
  • You can detect the downward trend of your blood pressure.

## The one-week protocol

The one-week protocol for checking blood pressure involves the following steps: Measure your blood pressure twice a day, at around the same time of day, for a week. Use a personal blood pressure monitor to take readings before or after meals, and after being awake for an hour. After your first day of monitoring, remove the first day's results from the records, because this day's readings are often unrepresentative. After that, calculate the average of the remaining readings, and use this as your new treatment goal. Continue with your blood pressure medication as prescribed by your doctor, and continue the one-week monitoring protocol. Reassess your blood pressure readings, and take note of any changes in your blood pressure. Once you have stable blood pressure readings, you can taper the frequency of your blood pressure checks, but it is very important to continue to check your blood pressure regularly to continue to control it. You should repeat the same week-long unit every few months to track any changes in your blood pressure readings. It is important to remember that more frequent checking of your blood pressure does more harm than good and provides no added benefit in the control of high blood pressure. The pattern of your blood pressure readings is more important than any single reading. The goal is to find a blood pressure monitoring frequency that gives you the feedback you need to safely control your blood pressure without any side effects.

## Timing

For good blood pressure monitoring, it is important to take your measurements at the same times every day. Your first reading should be taken in the morning, before you have had any coffee or taken any medication. This is the time of day when most people experience a morning surge in blood pressure, which has been linked to an increased risk of cardiovascular events. However, it is advisable to wait 30 minutes after the intake of caffeine, smoking, exercise, or alcohol, to ensure an accurate reading. If you take more than one reading a day, it is best to take it at the same time in the evening, because the time of day has an effect on blood pressure readings.

## Where readings go wrong

There are many ways to get inaccurate blood pressure readings. Setup errors alone can shift the readings by 10 points, without affecting your health. Here are some examples of factors that can increase your blood pressure readings:                            Cuff size: The cuff is the most overlooked error. Getting the wrong cuff size can bias the readings. If you use a cuff that is too small for your arm, it will give falsely high readings. In contrast, if the cuff is too big, it will give falsely low readings. You can avoid this problem by buying a cuff that fits your arm size. Most cuffs come in three sizes, but you can buy other sizes separately. Cuff placement: You should place the cuff directly on bare skin, not over clothing. If you put the cuff over clothing, it will give false readings because the cloth will compress under the cuff. Arm height: If you measure your blood pressure with your arm too high or too low, it will give false readings. Your arm should be even with your heart, so with the elbow slightly bent. Posture: Your posture is very important. Sit with your back supported and your feet flat on the floor. Rest 5 minutes and empty your bladder before measuring. Device: Wear-and-tear can affect any device. You should compare the results of your blood pressure device against clinic equipment to ensure accuracy. Place the monitor on the same arm as the arm that reads higher. Device type: If you use a wrist or finger blood pressure monitor, it is likely to give false readings. Use an upper-arm device instead. Usual traffic noise: The usual traffic noise in your environment will influence your readings. If you live close to a highway, try to measure your blood pressure in a quieter environment. Temperature: Room temperature changes of 5°F will affect your blood pressure readings. Try to measure your blood pressure at approximately the same temperature each day. Other factors: Pain, stress, anxiety, or exercise may also affect your blood pressure readings. The person taking the blood pressure should be as calm and quiet as possible, and avoid stressful conversations during the measurement.

## Reading the numbers

First, locate the larger number. This is your systolic pressure. Then, locate the smaller number. This is your diastolic pressure. Together, these two numbers give you a blood pressure reading. What should your systolic blood pressure be, and what should your diastolic blood pressure be? That depends on your age and health. Ask your doctor what your targets should be. In general, a blood pressure of less than 120 over less than 80 is considered normal. If your blood pressure averages 130 over 80 or above, take it to your doctor. You may be able to lower it with lifestyle changes, but do not adjust medications yourself. If your blood pressure is higher than 180 over 120, with symptoms, seek urgent care. If your blood pressure is higher than 180 over 120, without symptoms, recheck, and then call your doctor.

Do not adjust your blood pressure medications without asking your doctor first. Your blood pressure is a very important part of your long-term health, so take care of it with regular monitoring and a healthy lifestyle.

A single reading at the doctor’s office is just a snapshot of a patient’s BP levels. Home monitoring can help patients view their BP levels in a bigger picture, showing normal readings during ordinary days and helping patients stay calm when they are away from the stress of the clinic.
How Often Should You Measure?
If you have been diagnosed with high BP or your doctor has asked for blood pressure readings before an appointment or after you’ve started a new medication, take readings for about seven days. Take the readings twice a day, morning and evening. When you take readings, take two readings each time and wait one minute between the readings. Although there are many guidelines, it is advised that patients discard the first day’s results and average the results from the remaining days.
If your BP is well controlled, you can reduce your monitoring once you feel that your BP is stable. This could be one or two times a week or a one-week round every month or so, but only if your doctor advises it.
If you don’t have a diagnosis but are proactive, occasional checks could be beneficial, especially if you are over the age of 40 or have risk factors such to heart disease, diabetes, excess weight, or kidney disease. Occasional checks can help you stay aware of your BP.

Constant monitoring can fuel anxiety and cause you to overreact to normal fluctuations in your BP levels. BP naturally rises and falls throughout the day, so recognizing patterns in your readings is more important than the readings themselves.

High blood pressure is called the silent killer for a reason. It often has no symptoms, and if untreated, it can lead to serious health problems like heart attacks and strokes. That’s why it’s important to have your blood pressure checked regularly. But just getting a single reading at your doctor’s office isn’t enough. 

The problem is that a single reading doesn’t tell the whole story. It’s just a snapshot, taken in a highly controlled environment and after you’ve been waiting in a doctor’s office, which is inherently stressful. A single reading doesn’t show how your blood pressure varies throughout the day. And because blood pressure fluctuates all the time, it’s important to get an accurate measure of your overall average. 

That’s why experts recommend monitoring your blood pressure at home. Home monitoring shows the bigger picture: your normal, everyday blood pressure readings when you’re not under stress. In fact, the American Heart Association (AHA) recommends home monitoring for anyone diagnosed with high blood pressure. And they recommend it for anyone whose blood pressure is considered elevated, which means it’s higher than normal but not high enough for a diagnosis of high blood pressure. 

Home monitoring can also be helpful for people who have normal blood pressure. That’s because even people with normal blood pressure can develop high blood pressure as they get older. And high blood pressure increases the risk of heart disease and stroke. If you have any of the risk factors for high blood pressure, including a family history of high blood pressure, diabetes, obesity, or kidney disease, your doctor may recommend monitoring your blood pressure at home. 

How often should you check your blood pressure at home? 

The AHA recommends that people with high blood pressure check their blood pressure at home at least once a day, over the course of a week, before their appointment with their doctor. They recommend checking your blood pressure twice a day—morning and evening—taking two readings each time, one minute apart. 

Many guidelines recommend discarding the first reading of the day and averaging the remaining readings. 

Once your blood pressure is under control, you may be able to cut back on your home monitoring. Many experts recommend checking your blood pressure at home a few times a week, or once a month. Your doctor can advise you on how often you should check your blood pressure at home. 

If you don’t have high blood pressure but you have any of the risk factors for high blood pressure, or you’re over 40 years old, it’s a good idea to monitor your blood pressure at home occasionally. That way, you’ll know if you develop high blood pressure and can seek treatment early. 

How often should you check your blood pressure at home if you don’t have high blood pressure or any risk factors? 

Experts recommend checking your blood pressure at home occasionally, if you’re over 40 years old or have any of the risk factors for high blood pressure. You could do a week of readings every few months, or whenever you have a clinic reading that’s high. 

You could also check your blood pressure at home a few times a week, especially if you have any of the risk factors for high blood pressure. 

It’s a good idea to check your blood pressure at home when you feel ill, or if you’ve been very active or inactive, or if you’ve been eating a lot of salt. 

Why is it important to check your blood pressure at home at the same time each day? 

Checking your blood pressure at the same time each day makes it easier to compare your readings. It also gives you a better idea of how your blood pressure fluctuates throughout the day. 

The best time to check your blood pressure is in the morning, within an hour of waking up. That’s because blood pressure tends to surge in the morning. This morning surge is linked to heart attacks and strokes, so morning readings are especially valuable. 

When you’re checking your blood pressure at home, make sure you’re consistent about the time of day. 

How should you take a blood pressure reading at home? 

To get an accurate reading at home, it’s important to use the right technique. 

1. Rest first: sit quietly for at least five minutes before you take your blood pressure. Don’t talk, scroll on your phone, or watch anything stressful. 

2. Empty your bladder: a full bladder can raise your blood pressure reading. 

3. Avoid coffee, cigarettes, and exercise: don’t drink coffee, smoke, or exercise for at least 30 minutes before taking your blood pressure. 

4. Check the cuff size: using a cuff that’s too small can lead to falsely high readings, while using a cuff that’s too large can lead to falsely low readings. 

5. Position the cuff on bare skin: make sure the cuff is on bare skin, not over clothing. 

6. Place the cuff on the same arm each time, and make sure the arm is at heart level. 

7. Sit with your back supported and your feet flat on the floor. 

8. Relax your arm on a table with your palm up. Don’t cross your legs or dangle your feet. 

9. Don’t talk while you’re taking your blood pressure. 

10. Take two readings, one minute apart, and average the readings. 

11. Make sure you’re using a validated monitor: automatic upper-arm monitors are generally more accurate than wrist or finger devices. 

12. Choose a clinically validated device: make sure the device you use has been clinically validated. Many devices claim to be clinically validated, but they may not be. 

It’s a good idea to bring your home monitor to your doctor’s office so you can compare the readings from your home monitor to the readings from your doctor’s equipment. 

What do your blood pressure numbers mean? 

Blood pressure is measured in millimeters of mercury (mm Hg) and recorded as two numbers: systolic pressure (the top number) and diastolic pressure (the bottom number). 

For example, if your systolic pressure is 120 and your diastolic pressure is 80, you would write your blood pressure as 120/80 mm Hg. 

What do the numbers mean? 

Systolic pressure (the top number): the pressure in your blood vessels when your heart beats. 

Diastolic pressure (the bottom number): the pressure in your blood vessels when your heart rests between beats. 

What do the numbers mean for you? 

Normal blood pressure: less than 120/80 mm Hg 

Elevated blood pressure: systolic between 120–129 and diastolic less than 80 

Stage 1 high blood pressure: systolic 130–139 or diastolic 80–89 

Stage 2 high blood pressure: systolic 140 or higher or diastolic 90 or higher 

Hypertensive crisis (emergency care required): systolic 180 or higher or diastolic 120 or higher 

If you have high blood pressure, your doctor will recommend a treatment plan based on your health and your blood pressure numbers. 

The goal of treatment is to lower your blood pressure to below 140/90 mm Hg. For some people, the goal is an even lower blood pressure. 

What if your blood pressure is very high? 

If your blood pressure is very high, seek medical attention right away. A very high blood pressure reading can be a sign of a hypertensive crisis, which is an emergency. 

What are the symptoms of a hypertensive crisis? 

A hypertensive crisis can cause: 

- Chest pain 

- Shortness of breath 

- Severe headache 

- Vision changes 

- Difficulty speaking 

- Numbness or weakness 

- Confusion 

If you have any of these symptoms, call 911 or go to your nearest emergency department. 

What if your blood pressure is very low? 

A very low blood pressure reading can be a sign of a medical emergency, especially if you have symptoms like: 

- Confusion 

- Dizziness or lightheadedness 

- Fainting 

- Blurred vision 

- Nausea

# Language Programmes at East Otago High School

East Otago High School teaches two languages, German and te reo Māori, across Years 7 to 10, and each stage of the programme has its own job. The early years introduce both languages. Year 9 adds structure and may narrow the focus. By Year 10, students who choose to continue are working at a faster pace and towards a clear purpose. The school offers both languages for a reason: one connects students to the place they live, and the other connects them to the wider world.

## How the years step up

In Years 7 and 8, the aim is exposure, not intensity. Students meet both languages without pressure, and the point is to get them curious rather than to push them hard.

Year 9 brings more structure. Lessons become more organised, and students may begin to narrow their study to one language. That choice follows from what they have experienced in the first two years.

Year 10 is an option subject. Students select it themselves, which changes the character of the class. Those who are there have chosen to be, and the pace is faster as a result. Each step builds on the one before, so a student arriving in Year 10 has already spent time with the language, learned its basic structures and decided it is worth pursuing.

## German: from taster to travel

German begins as a taster in Years 7 and 8. The format is playful, designed to let students try the language and enjoy it before anything demands formal study.

Year 9 is where the real grammar arrives. The playful approach gives way to the rules that make the language work, and students start to see how sentences are built rather than just repeating phrases. It is a noticeable shift, and it is the point at which a student decides whether German is for them.

In Year 10, the course has a dual aim: NCEA credits and preparation for travel. The two goals support each other. The skills that matter for assessment are also the ones a student needs to get around in a German-speaking country, and the course keeps both in view.

Throughout, students work with authentic materials. They meet German as it is actually used, not only as it appears in a textbook. That keeps the language connected to real people and real situations, and it gives the travel aim some substance, since students are already practising with the kind of material they would encounter abroad.

## Te Reo Māori, rooted in place

What sets the te reo Māori programme apart is that it is local from day one, not generic. The pepeha is a good example. Students do not just learn the form of an introduction; they place themselves within their own landscape and connections.

The programme also teaches the Kāi Tahu dialect. Where other dialects use ng, Kāi Tahu uses k, which is why Ngāi Tahu becomes Kāi Tahu. It is a small detail, but it shows what local means in practice: students learn the language as it is spoken in their own region.

This matters because it makes the language belong to the students' own surroundings. They are not learning something distant. They are learning the speech of the place where they go to school.

Year 9 keeps that focus. Students work with stories of the coastline and begin writing their own sentences, so they are moving from recognising the language to using it, and doing so about a place they know.

In Year 10, the programme adds formal register and marae tikanga. Students learn how the language is used on formal occasions, and how to conduct themselves in the setting where it carries the most weight.

The payoff is the role of marae liaison, and it is the strongest point in the programme. Everything before it leads here. The local vocabulary, the dialect, the stories of the coastline and the formal register all prepare students to take on a real responsibility, one that carries meaning beyond the classroom. A student who can speak with the right dialect, in the right register and with an understanding of tikanga is equipped to help the school and the marae work together. The role is not an exercise or a simulation. It places students in a genuine position of service, where their language skills matter to other people.

That is where the programme ends: with a working relationship between the school and mana whenua, carried in part by its students.

At East Otago High School, we are on track with a goal of embedding languages into the curriculum. We aim to achieve this by offering two languages to our students at Years 7–10. Each year level has a key language role. The Year 7 role is exposure, the Year 8 role is exploration, the Year 9 role is selection, and the Year 10 role is choice. We acknowledge the two languages chosen for our school are situated in the two contexts in which we operate – local and global. German and Māori. We are keen to increase students’ understanding that languages and cultures are interconnected and not isolated entities. This is evident through recent conversations with our Year 9 students and feedback from parents.

Our students begin their language learning by exploring the different languages through Year 7 and 8. At this stage, students are exposed to German and Māori. Students are given the opportunity to learn in playful, authentic contexts. These contexts include picture books, games, interactive activities, songs and videos. The Year 9 role focuses on the selection of languages by students. The content of Māori and German at this year level aims to provide students with a solid foundation of language structures and skills. German is taught through a grammar-based format. This approach is ideal for the German language, as it allows students to access the language at a deeper level through sentence construction. This also allows students to select vocabulary and grammar structures that are relevant to their learning and interests. For example, students may learn how to talk about their interests by constructing sentences in German. Māori is taught through a focused and thematic approach. This means that students learn about a specific topic in detail, giving them the opportunity to build language through meaningful interactions. Māori is taught through authentic materials to develop our students’ understanding of local languages and cultures and how they differ from others. These materials include stories, songs and videos.

In Year 10, students are given the opportunity to further develop their language skills through choice. German and Māori become option subjects at this level. At this stage, students may choose to continue or select their preferred language based on their interests. The Year 10 role aims to give students the opportunity to develop language skills at a faster rate due to the self-selected nature of the course. Students may begin their language learning at this stage, as they have the option to learn a language that may not have been taught at their school. The learning of German and Māori at this year level continues to develop students’ understanding of the world around them.

German Year 10 has a dual aim, to complete NCEA Level 1 and 2 credits and to build language and cultural competency for travel. German Year 10 students learn in an authentic learning environment. They are exposed to authentic materials in order to build their German language skills. Students have the opportunity to visit Germany in order to engage in authentic language interactions.

The Māori Year 10 role focuses on the formal register of Māori. Students learn about the traditional patterns of speech used when talking to elders and other members of the community. Marae tikanga is another focus at this year level. Students learn how to conduct themselves on marae and interact with whanau through the use of protocols and procedures. This year is integral to the growth of our students’ understanding of mana whenua and how it can be used as a way to connect with local communities and whānau.

We are also keen to increase our students’ understanding that languages and cultures are interconnected and not isolated entities. We have been given the opportunity to collaborate with our local marae through our Māori language programme. Our aim is to further develop our students’ cultural competency by engaging with a local marae. This will give students the opportunity to further develop their Māori language skills by communicating with whanau. We believe this will also strengthen the relationship between our school and marae, giving our students and whanau the opportunity to develop their cultural competency through meaningful relationships.

At East Otago High School, all of the Year 7–10 pupils learn two languages – one is English and the other is the choice of the student. Each stage has a specific job that must be completed to help the student learn the language. One language is learned because of the importance of being bilingual in New Zealand. Another language is chosen to help the student to communicate with friends or family who may speak another language, or simply to travel and communicate overseas. The only requirement to learn a language at East Otago High School is to listen, understand, speak, read and write in both languages. If the teacher feels that the student is not trying hard enough then they will be moved to a lower group until they improve.

## How the years step up

In the first two years of learning a language, students have a choice to learn how to speak and understand the language at a basic level. As the years progress, the way the student learns a language becomes more structured, and students who are not interested in their second language can choose to only learn one language. In the last two years, students can choose to learn the language that interests them the most, or they can choose to drop the language completely. By Year 10, the option of a language will be entirely up to the student.

## German: from taster to travel

The German language is offered at East Otago High School to help students become bilingual. During the first two years of learning German, students are introduced to the language in a fun and playful format. In the second and third years, students learn how to read and speak the language in a more structured and intense manner, but they are still able to choose the language that suits them best. This allows students the freedom to decide if they want to continue learning the language, or whether they would like to pick another language. In the last two years, students are given the choice to study German for the NCEA exam, or they can choose to study German to learn how to travel to a German-speaking country. To help the students learn as much as possible about the German language, the school has provided its students with authentic German materials to use.

## Te Reo Māori, rooted in place

At East Otago High School, students learn two languages. The first language is English, but all students at East Otago High School also learn Te Reo Māori. Te Reo Māori has been taught at East Otago High School for over a decade, and it is the only language programme at East Otago High School that introduces students to local place names and stories from the area. To teach students how to read, write and speak the language, students are encouraged to use the local area and traditional stories as examples. The teaching of Te Reo Māori has become an increasingly important part of the school’s curriculum because East Otago High School is located in an area that is rich in history, culture and stories. To help students become bilingual, the school has provided its students with authentic Te Reo Māori materials to use. To help students learn and understand the language, teachers have developed a range of interactive teaching techniques that have been proven to be successful for students who are learning Te Reo Māori at East Otago High School.

claude.text:
# Liability Without a Contract: Data, Defamation, and Defective Products

Most people think of legal exposure as something that begins with a signed agreement. You promise to deliver, the other side promises to pay, and if someone breaks the deal, a court sorts it out. But a large share of business liability works differently. The duty you owe comes from the law itself, not from anything you agreed to.

That distinction matters because it means you can be exposed to people with whom you never signed a thing. A customer whose personal data you held, a person named in something your company published online, and a user injured by a product you sold can all bring claims. None of them needs a contract with you. The law imposes the obligation, and breaching it can be enough to put your business in front of a court, with no document anywhere in the picture.

## Why intent matters

The real business payoff of understanding intent lies in two places: punitive damages and the insurance gap. Intentional wrongs can open the door to punitive damages, and insurance often does not cover them, which leaves the business paying out of its own pocket.

In this context, intent refers to the act, not the damage. The question is whether you meant to do the thing, not whether you meant for harm to result.

Negligence, by contrast, requires a duty, a breach of that duty, causation, and damages.

## Data custodian risk

The strongest point in cyber liability is that your exposure comes from being a custodian of data, not a perpetrator of its theft. You do not have to be the one who attacked anyone. Holding the information is enough to create responsibility for protecting it.

When a breach occurs, the consequences tend to arrive on two fronts. Affected individuals can bring negligence claims, arguing that the business failed to protect what it was entrusted with. At the same time, regulators can take an interest in how the data was handled. A single incident can therefore produce private litigation and regulatory scrutiny together.

This ties directly back to the point about intent. Nobody has to have wanted the breach to happen, and the business does not need to have acted deliberately. The claim rests on a failure of care in how the data was kept, not on a wrongful purpose. A company that never imagined being targeted can still find itself answering for what happened to the information in its hands.

## Online defamation

Posts that damage someone's reputation can amount to libel, because written statements published online are treated as written defamation. That makes ordinary business activity a potential source of liability.

Businesses face particular risk in several areas, and the same care applies to any public statement that could harm another party's reputation.

Section 230 draws an important line between who wrote something and who hosted it. The author of a defamatory post can be held liable. The platform or host that carries it usually cannot. That protection for hosts does not shield the person who actually wrote the statement.

## Strict products liability

Under strict products liability, care is no defense. A seller can take every reasonable precaution and still be held responsible if the product turns out to be defective. The rationale, in one line, is that the business selling the product is better placed to absorb and spread the cost of injuries than the person who was hurt.

The plaintiff still carries a burden. They must show that the product was defective and that the defect caused the harm. Defects come in three types: manufacturing defects, design defects, and warning defects.

Two of those deserve particular attention. A design defect means the product's very design makes it unreasonably dangerous, even when it was built exactly as intended. A warning defect means the product lacked adequate instructions or cautions about its risks. In both cases, flawless execution on the factory floor does not help.

Finally, this liability reaches retailers too. That is the key point for businesses that do not manufacture anything. If you sell a defective product, you can be liable even though you did not design or build it.

## Where defendants push back

Strict liability is not automatic. Defendants have arguments available, and several are worth knowing.

Misuse is one. The hinge is foreseeability: if the way the product was used could reasonably have been anticipated, the argument weakens considerably, whereas truly unforeseeable misuse may help the defense.

Alteration is another. If someone changed the product after it left your hands, and that change caused the harm, the defendant can argue the defect was not theirs.

Even so, one point deserves emphasis. Complying with regulations does not provide a safe harbor. A product can satisfy every applicable requirement and still be found defective, so regulatory compliance alone is not a guarantee against liability.

base.text:
In the absence of a signed agreement, it is a myth that a company has no liability to its customers. In reality, liability comes from the law, not from an agreement. Furthermore, while it’s easy to imagine the obvious business losses that can result from not having a written agreement, the stakes are very concrete when you add in exposure with no signed document. The real business payoff is reducing costs and improving the bottom line. The cost reductions come from reducing risk exposure, and the profit comes from being able to sell insurance to cover what you can’t eliminate. It is possible to reduce exposure and lower premiums—and, with that reduction, close the insurance coverage gap.

Most liability exposures don’t require intent, so you can think of liability as coming in three flavors: duty, breach, and harm. Duty means that the law imposes a duty on you to take action or refrain from taking action. A common duty is the duty to warn of a foreseeable risk. Breach means that you’ve failed to follow the duty. Harm means that you’ve caused harm to someone. Harm is the third element that completes the cause of action, or the claim. With no intention, you didn’t mean to cause the harm. With no breach, you didn’t break the duty. With no duty, you don’t have to do anything. (Duty comes from law, not from agreement.)

Why Intent Matters

Intent is only one element of negligence. Negligence has four elements: duty, breach, harm, and proximate cause. Proximate cause means that the harm resulted from the breach. Causation is a necessity in every cause of action. For the business audience, the key is that intent is not required for breach. The act that was undertaken or not taken is what matters. Intent does matter for punitives, which are damages awarded by the jury or judge that are intended to punish the defendant and not just compensate the plaintiff. We’ll talk about this a little more later.

Data Custodian Risk

One area where intent is irrelevant is the custodian of data. You may not be the person who hacked the data, but you’re still in breach if you didn’t follow industry standard security practices. A third party’s breach might not trigger your duty to warn, depending on the data and your industry, but it likely triggers your duty to warn your customers about the third party’s breach, if you were made aware of it. Not telling your customers is a breach of the duty to warn. You can’t get away from this kind of liability through an agreement, because the duty comes from the law, not from an agreement. This kind of breach can result in regulatory action.

Online Defamation

Another form of negligence with no intent requirement is defamation. With defamation, you say something that isn’t true that harms someone’s reputation. It can be libel (written, such as in a blog post) or slander (spoken). The latter is easier to avoid, because it’s hard to find a transcript. For libel, on the other hand, you need to pay attention to the content you display. For example, there are sites with comments posted by customers that include defamatory statements. You’re not the author, so you’re not the defamer, right? Not quite.

Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act limits your liability for defamation if you host content created by someone else. There is no limitation, however, if you create the content yourself. One thing to keep in mind is that content doesn’t have to be words. For example, pictures can be considered content. The case that created this distinction was a picture of a mushroom cloud. The judge found that the picture couldn’t stand by itself as content, because you needed words to make the point that the city had been bombed. However, in the subsequent case, the judge found that a picture of a woman in a bathtub, by itself, with no text, was content that could be defamatory.

What are the business implications? If you host comments from customers, they’re responsible for their statements. If you put up content, however, you’re responsible.

Strict Products Liability

A third area is strict product liability. Strict liability means that you don’t have to prove that the manufacturer was negligent. If the product causes harm, you get sued unless one of the exceptions applies. The exceptions are: the manufacturer warned of the risk, or you’re not the intended user, or there was a misuse that was unforeseeable. Misuse can be an interesting area.

For example, a common scenario is a restaurant serving a beverage that’s too hot and causing burns. The defense is that the customer has to be careful, or else you’d have to put a warning on every cup. The counterargument is that the risk is foreseeable. Put differently, how many people would have to burn themselves before it becomes foreseeable? The answer is a small number. The answer is not that it has to be common. Common means it happens often. Foreseeable means that it would happen at least once. Judges and juries are often lenient on defendants, so you shouldn’t depend on that defense, because once is enough to get you sued, regardless of whether the judge or jury finds you liable.

Where Defendants Push Back

You could be thinking that it’s not realistic to try to eliminate all risk. Your business will shut down if you try to eliminate all risk. That’s exactly right. The goal isn’t to eliminate all risk; that’s not possible. The goal is to minimize risk to a reasonable level by setting acceptable standards of performance. Setting the standard is the tricky part.

The most common scenario for a defendant to push back is strict liability. If the manufacturer warns of a risk, and you ignore the warning and cause harm, the manufacturer isn’t liable. In essence, the manufacturer tells you what to do to avoid harm, and if you don’t follow the directions, that’s your problem. The rationale behind this exception is that you had a choice to avoid the harm, and you chose not to do it.

Another common scenario for the manufacturer to push back is that the harm resulted from a misuse of the product. It’s not the manufacturer’s fault that you did something wrong with the product that it wasn’t intended to do. One classic example is the person who used a chainsaw as a pogo stick and got injured. The chainsaw wasn’t intended to be a pogo stick, so the manufacturer isn’t liable. This exception is sometimes stated as foreseeability of the misuse. If your chainsaw has a warning that says, “This product is not a pogo stick,” then you’ve done your duty to warn. You can’t foresee everything, and if you did, you couldn’t sell anything. The duty is to warn about what you can foresee.

A related exception is that the product was altered after it left the manufacturer’s hands. Then it’s no longer the manufacturer’s problem. The manufacturer made a product that didn’t hurt anyone. It’s not the manufacturer’s problem that you went and changed it.

You could be thinking that the customer’s misuse or modification puts you in the clear. Not so fast. First, the failure to warn or to provide instructions might be a breach of duty. Second, not all regulatory requirements are related to customer safety. Some are related to manufacturing or supply chain integrity. With those, you still have a duty even if the customer changed the product after it left your hands. Third, you might have a duty to warn or provide instructions about how to avoid the harm.
