The law imposes liability on persons even if they are not parties to a contract. Contracts serve to define rights and duties among parties who have agreed to its terms. There are situations where liability arises without a contract.

## Why intent matters

The most important concept in liability law is intent, because intent is what underlies an act, not the damage it causes. Intent is the touchstone in liability law, and is defined in the law as reckless indifference. For liability to be proven, it must be demonstrated that the accused was aware of the risk, but did not care, and went ahead and acted anyway.

## Data custodian risk

The strongest defense to cyber liability is that the defendant is a custodian of data, not the perpetrator. The insurance industry has recognized this distinction, and has created a number of products that cover custodians, but not perpetrators. If the defendant has breached the duty owed to the plaintiff, and thereby has committed negligence, then the defendant will be liable for the damages caused.

## Online defamation

Defamation is a term that applies to statements made by one person that tend to lower the reputation of another. A posting online may be libelous if it is untrue, and is published with the intent to harm. Certain members of the community, such as innkeepers, public utilities, and others, are subject to stricter defamation standards than others.

## Strict products liability

Strict products liability is the modern term for the ancient legal concept that the seller of a product is liable for injuries caused by the product, even in the absence of any action that would be considered intentional or negligent. Strict products liability protects manufacturers, sellers, and even retailers of defective products. Unlike traditional negligence law, strict products liability does not require a plaintiff to prove any actual negligence by the defendant. It only requires that the product sold was defective, and that the defect was the cause of the plaintiff's injury.

## Where defendants push back

Strict liability is not automatic liability. The product must actually be defective in some way, and the defendant must have had knowledge of the defect, or the defect must have been foreseeable to the defendant. The plaintiff's case is very strong when the product is defective in design, but more difficult to prove when the defect arises from a defective warning. The manufacturer of the product has a duty to warn consumers of the potential hazards, and if the manufacturer fails to do so, then the defendant will be liable. This duty to warn reaches retailers as well as manufacturers, and even after-sale alterations and modifications.

The law imposes liability on persons without a contract, in situations involving: first, defamation and invasion of privacy, where speech concerns someone else; second, hazardous products, where distribution exposes everyone to injury; and third, automobiles, where the possibility of injury to others comes with the purchase.

The real business payoff of avoiding liability without a contract comes from the punishment of punitive damages and the insurance gap. Intent matters in liability because the question of whether the act was willful or negligent (or whether damage resulted) is irrelevant to the intent element. The four-element test of negligence is: (1) a duty, (2) a breach of the duty, (3) a causal connection between the breach and the injury, and (He) harm.
Duty of care
The case of legal duty becomes clear when one considers that the common law imposes a duty to avoid the risk of foreseeable harm. A person who steps into the street in front of an approaching car, even though the driver is unable to stop, is said to have assumed the risk, and so is not entitled to recover from the driver. But if the driver is unable to stop because he is drunk, the driver will be liable to the pedestrian. The drunk driver has breached his duty to exercise reasonable care by failing to keep a proper lookout for pedestrians.

## Data custodian risk

The strongest legal point for cyber exposure as a custodian, rather than as a perpetrator, lies in the fact that custodians have no intent to cause damage. In fact, custodians have a duty to act with care to avoid causing damage. In other words, custodians have two different duties – a duty to act with care to avoid damage, and also a duty to avoid acting with the intent to cause damage.
The first duty is in the case of negligence claims, and the second duty is in the case of intentional damage. In the case of intentional damage, if the custodian has a motive to act with intent to cause damage, the custodian’s duty to act with care is also breached. The custodian’s duty to act with care is breached in the case of intentional damage. The custodian’s duty to avoid acting with intent to cause damage is breached in both the case of negligence and the case of intentional damage.

## Online defamation

The creation of defamatory posts on social media can lead to claims of defamation, both for libel and for slander (spoken defamation). Although the liability will fall mostly on the author, and not on the platform, platforms are required to adopt a content management system to address user complaints about defamatory content. The liability risk from defamation can be reduced by adopting and documenting a content moderation system, which includes warning users about the consequences of posting defamatory content, having a system for receiving complaints, issuing take-down notices, and having an appeals process.

## Strict products liability

Strict products liability is one of the most important concepts in product liability law. It means that it is not necessary to prove that the manufacturer was careless – carelessness is not a defense. It is sufficient to prove that the defective product caused the injury, and that the product left the manufacturer’s control in a defective condition. There are three types of defects, which may be related to design, warning, or manufacturing.
Product defect liability exists for any seller who places a product into the stream of commerce, so it reaches the retailer, who is also liable. For a non-manufacturer, the only time this link is not present is where the retailer has no knowledge about the defect. In that case, liability is limited to the dealer or distributor, who is in a better position to control the defective product.

This article discusses the differences between tort and contract law, with particular emphasis on the liability of businesses for harms caused by their products. A key aspect of tort law is its "duty of care," whereby a person has an obligation to act reasonably in order to avoid harming others. In contrast, contract law requires a party to perform a specific duty as set forth in an agreement. The article describes the consequences of committing an intentional tort, which may include punitive damages, versus an unintentional tort, which typically results in only compensatory damages. Additionally, the article provides examples of common torts such as negligence and defamation, as well as the distinction between strict liability and products liability. Finally, the article outlines common defenses available to defendants in tort cases.

Discussion Questions:
1. What are some examples of intentional torts that might arise in a business context?
2. How does the "duty of care" apply to businesses?
3. What are some ways that businesses can limit their exposure to liability for injuries caused by their products?
4. Under what circumstances might a business be liable for injuries caused by a third party's use of its product?

Answer to Discussion Question 1: Examples of intentional torts that might arise in a business context include assault, battery, false imprisonment, and intentional infliction of emotional distress. These types of torts often occur when an employee of a business acts outside of his or her authority or commits an act of violence against a customer or coworker.

Answer to Discussion Question 2: The "duty of care" applies to businesses in various ways, depending on the nature of their operations. For example, businesses that manufacture products have a duty to ensure that those products are safe for consumers to use. Businesses that provide services also have a duty to ensure that they do not negligently cause harm to their customers. Additionally, businesses have a duty to protect the privacy of customer data and to take reasonable steps to prevent data breaches.

Answer to Discussion Question 3: Some ways that businesses can limit their exposure to liability for injuries caused by their products include conducting thorough testing and safety inspections, obtaining adequate insurance coverage, and providing clear instructions and warnings regarding the proper use of the product. Businesses can also limit their exposure by ensuring that their employees are properly trained and supervised.

Answer to Discussion Question 4: A business might be liable for injuries caused by a third party's use of its product if the business had a duty to prevent the injury from occurring. For example, if a business sold a defective product to a distributor, who then sold it to a consumer, the business might be liable if the consumer was injured by the product. Another example would be if a business failed to take reasonable steps to ensure the safety of its premises, and a third party was injured as a result.

Key Takeaways:
- The primary distinction between tort and contract law is that contract law focuses on agreements between parties, while tort law addresses harms caused by one party to another.
- Intentional torts involve deliberate actions that cause harm, whereas unintentional torts result from negligence or other forms of carelessness.
- Strict liability is a form of liability that exists regardless of whether a party exercised reasonable care in avoiding the harm.
- Products liability refers to liability for harms caused by defective products, including manufacturing defects, design defects, and failure to warn about known risks.

# Keep the Maternal Mortality Task Force. Then Act on It.

Extending the task force is the wrong place to stop. A review panel can tell Texas why mothers are dying, but a diagnosis is not a cure, and the cure belongs to the Legislature. Lawmakers are heading into a special session, and they should renew the task force quickly, without drama or delay. Then they should use the same session to act on what it has already told them. Keeping the panel alive is the easy part. The harder part is doing something with what it finds.

## Why the review matters

The task force's core value is that it reviews deaths one case at a time. That matters because a death label hides what actually happened. A record that names a single cause of death says nothing about the missed appointment, the untreated condition, or the coverage that ran out. Case-by-case review brings those things into view, and they are the places where a policy can intervene.

Critics point to errors in the data, and they are right that errors exist. But the answer to imperfect data is better data, not no review at all. Flawed numbers are a reason to look more closely at individual cases, not to stop looking.

If the task force lapses, the cost is high and hard to undo. Case files go unreviewed, patterns go unseen, and an institution that took years to build has to be assembled again from scratch. Letting the panel lapse would mean Texas stops learning why its mothers die.

## Who dies

Start with the ratio: the gap in death rates between groups of Texas mothers is not a rounding error. The tempting explanation is class, and it does not close that gap. The causes are familiar and often treatable. Untreated hypertension is one, the kind of condition case review turns up behind a death label that names something else. Overdose is another.

## The 60-day cliff

Medicaid pays for roughly half of the births in Texas. That coverage comes with a cliff. Sixty days after delivery, it ends.

The task force's key finding is that deaths cluster after that window closes. Overdose is the clearest postpartum example. A mother who gets treatment during pregnancy often loses it once the baby arrives, because the coverage that paid for it was tied to the pregnancy. Treatment stops just as the risks of the postpartum months continue.

Texas makes this worse than most states. It has not expanded Medicaid, and its eligibility limits are strict. A woman who loses pregnancy coverage at 60 days has few places to turn. She is likely to fall straight into the ranks of the uninsured, with no way to pay for the care she still needs.

The consequence is that mothers die in the months when the state has stopped paying attention. Of everything the task force could recommend, one fix deserves the most pressure: extend postpartum coverage to 12 months. It is the direct answer to the finding. If deaths cluster after the 60-day window, the window is what needs to change. Twelve months of coverage would keep treatment going for the women who now lose it, including those with hypertension and those in recovery from addiction.

## The real test

Renewing the task force is an easy vote. Nobody will campaign against studying maternal deaths, and a unanimous show of support costs lawmakers nothing. The hard test comes after that vote, when the findings call for spending money and changing the rules.

The task force has done its part. It has named the problem and shown where the deaths fall. The question for this session is whether the Legislature will do its part.

Reformers who want to reduce the number of women dying during and after childbirth scored an important victory recently. The Legislature approved funding to keep the Maternal Mortality and Morbidity Task Force going.

That's great. But the task force is an extension of an existing government commission, the Quality Improvement Commission. And while the task force has had success, that's not the main reason Gov. Greg Abbott and legislative leaders should have extended its life.

The task force, for the most part, just collects information. Its work is valuable, and it deserves the support of everyone who cares about women's health.

The task force collects data on maternal deaths, and it analyzes those deaths to see what caused them. But the ultimate goal isn't just to gather information. The task force's work is supposed to lead to changes that lower the state's maternal mortality rate, which is higher than the national rate and ranks near the bottom among states.

The Legislature and the governor should already be trying to lower the state's maternal mortality rate. That's what the Legislature and governor are elected to do.

The Legislature isn't just a data-gathering body. It's a policymaking body.

The task force's work is important. But even its final report this year didn't try to directly address the root causes of maternal mortality. It didn't, for example, propose that the state expand Medicaid coverage to pregnant women or that it give women more flexibility in accessing health care after their babies are born.

The task force is trying to figure out how to reduce maternal mortality. But the Legislature shouldn't be waiting for a task force to give them the answers. Policymakers should be doing what they were elected to do: Make the tough choices that will help women stay safe during and after their pregnancies.

The Legislature could fund paid family leave, and it could expand Medicaid coverage to pregnant women and their newborns. It could make certain that more women get their pregnancies on track by ensuring they get the care they need when they need it. And it could ensure that more women have time off from work after giving birth.

The task force is important. But the Legislature shouldn't leave all the policymaking up to a government commission. The Legislature should be making the hard choices itself.

The problem with the Maternal Mortality Task Force, despite good work on its behalf by the Texas Legislature, is that it hasn't done anything yet. It's just beginning to diagnose what's wrong with Texas' maternal health system, which has the country's fourth highest rate of maternal death. Until it issues its report and the Legislature responds, this task force is a study in motion. Completing the task is the Legislature's job. Acting on it is the Legislature's job, too, and that requires calling a special session. Until the task force completes its work, though, it won't have recommendations that the Legislature can adopt. So let's not put the brakes on anything until the task force's report is out.

## Why the review matters

The best way to make sure that the maternal death diagnosis is right is to review each case. When a woman dies during or shortly after pregnancy, the state already does this, but only in a small number of cases. In Texas, a woman has to die for seven days after birth, for example, for the review to apply. The task force wants to extend that review to cover at least 50 percent of all maternal deaths - that's about 13 deaths a year. The point is, if you don't review each death, you might miss something. And that's what a case in Texas showed. A case with a complicated medical background, but with one detail that a review might have caught. And a detail that has made some lawmakers question whether the state's maternal mortality rate is as high as the data show.

## Who dies

The task force's report says that between 2010 and 2013, 1 in 6 of the women who died were Black, but that Black women make up just 12 percent of the state's population. It also says that Black women are three times more likely to die from maternal health complications than other women. The task force says that a major cause is untreated hypertension, which often goes untested or untreated in pregnant women, but which can be very dangerous during pregnancy. In the case that's at the center of this review, the task force says that the woman had high blood pressure, but she had not received medical care that would have identified it. That's the point of the review. If it had happened, it might have saved her life.

## The 60-day cliff

The Task Force's report says that most maternal deaths happen between 60 days before a birth and 60 days after one - what it calls "the maternal mortality cliff". And it says that many of those deaths happen in Texas, where Medicaid covers more than half of all births. About half of the women who die of maternal complications are covered by Medicaid. And Texas has rejected the Medicaid expansion, which would have extended coverage to more women and cut down on the number of uninsured women. As a result, Medicaid isn't available to more than half of women who would be eligible for it under the expansion. The Task Force's report says that deaths happen on both sides of that cliff, with the majority of them after birth and in the postpartum period - the first 12 months after a baby is born. That's when the state stops paying for medical treatment, and because of that, women don't get the care that they need.

## The real test

There are lawmakers who say that the Task Force has already done enough. They want to keep it and make sure that it continues to do its work. They're right, but that's not the hard part. The hard part will come when the report is out and the Legislature has to decide what to do about it. There are lawmakers who are worried that the Task Force will propose policies that are too extreme, or that it won't be able to agree on what to do. And there are lawmakers who say that the Task Force doesn't do enough, that the report is just a way to "study the problem to death". Those lawmakers are wrong. For starters, the Task Force isn't a policymaking body; it just makes recommendations. But the real test will come when the Task Force has made its recommendations and the Legislature has to decide what to do about it. That's the hard part. That's when the Task Force will have to make the case for the policies that it's recommending, and the state lawmakers will have to decide whether they want to adopt them.

The task force has found that Texas needs to fix its prenatal care system. It is the state's priority now. The Legislature should fix this problem quickly, but it should also do much, much more.

The Legislature should pass a bill that requires the review. Then it should start fixing the rest of the problems.

The Legislature should also require that hospitals in rural areas provide more staff and more training, so that they can provide the type of care that the task force recommends.

The Legislature should require hospitals to report each time they do an ultrasound, so that it has the data to decide when to do more ultrasounds.

And the Legislature should pass laws that require hospitals to track the results of their own care. The task force found that hospitals do not do that now. If the task force had not been able to get the data, we would not know that the hospitals were failing.

The Legislature should pass laws to require that hospitals track their own results and publish them

Texas is asking itself whether it should continue studying why mothers die. The answer is yes. But we shouldn’t stop here.

base13.text:
This summer, the Texas Legislature is facing a question: Should it reauthorize a task force created to study why mothers die in childbirth?

The answer is yes, but the task force, now set to expire on Sept. 1, should be reauthorized for just a year, with a plan to return it to the Legislature next spring for a full review of what comes next.

When the Texas Maternal Mortality and Morbidity Task Force was created in 2013, it was to investigate a crisis: Texas had the highest maternal mortality rate in the developed world. A 2013 study found that nearly 50 women per 100,000 births died in Texas, compared with an average of 12 women per 100,000 in other high-income countries.

That’s a problem for a state that prides itself on having the best health care in the world.

As the task force was working, the data got worse. The state Department of State Health Services released a report in 2016 saying that the death rate had increased to 57 women per 100,000 live births. The data is still under review, and the death rate could fall when it’s finalized. But even the lower number is staggering.

The task force’s work has been crucial in sorting out the causes of these deaths. It has brought together physicians, nurses, epidemiologists, public health experts and maternal health experts to review the deaths case by case. It has helped identify problems with how the state records maternal deaths, including how pregnancy is recorded on death certificates and how the data is coded. Some of the deaths previously reported as maternal deaths were reclassified as cardiac arrests, for example, or overdoses.

The task force is working to correct these data problems, but its work is far from finished. Because of the data problems, many of the deaths that occurred during the time the task force has been working have yet to be fully reviewed. The task force’s work has already uncovered preventable causes of death. And the task force has identified areas that need more research, including the racial disparities in maternal mortality.

The task force has recommended several important changes, including a plan to provide free long-acting birth control to any woman who requests it. But there are many more things that need to be done to prevent deaths, including expanding Medicaid coverage to more pregnant women, ensuring that women have access to substance abuse treatment and mental health care, and expanding access to health care in rural areas.

The task force has been working since 2013. The Legislature should extend it for another year, giving lawmakers a chance to decide whether they want to continue funding the task force. But they should also take the recommendations of the task force to heart and act on them.

This summer, the Legislature will have a chance to do the easy thing — pass an extension for the task force. But lawmakers will also have a chance to do the hard thing and act on what the task force has uncovered. That would make a real difference in the lives of Texas mothers.

claude.text:
# Seven Words: What Can Only Be Said

[Gibran's provocation, quoted in one line.]

Here is the rule this piece rests on: some things exist only when they are said. No act can stand in for them. A gesture can accompany them, support them, even make them believable, but it cannot be them. The saying is the thing itself.

Action is eloquent, and I won't pretend otherwise. A hand on a shoulder, a meal cooked, a door held open: these speak, and sometimes they speak better than sentences do. But eloquence is not the same as precision, and the words below are about precision. They are the ones where the doing falls short.

Look at the list I ended up with, and notice what is missing. Nothing on it is pointable. You cannot gesture at any of these words and say, "There, that one." Every item on the list is something you can only hear, say, or take on trust. I didn't plan that. It was what remained once I removed everything an action could do.

## Love

This is the strongest case for the rule, because the acts that seem to carry love are so often ambiguous. Someone drives across town for you. Is that love, duty, habit, guilt? Someone remembers how you take your coffee. Is that devotion, or just good memory? The act alone cannot say.

Saying it is a risk. That is part of why we avoid it. Implication is comfortable: it lets us mean something without owning it, and it lets the other person decline to notice. Said aloud, the word leaves no room to hide. It can be heard and answered, and it can be refused. That exposure is exactly what makes it count.

None of this makes the acts worthless. The drive, the coffee, the quiet attention are all real. But on their own they are evidence waiting for a verdict. The word is the verdict. Once it is spoken, every earlier act is reread in its light, and what was ambiguous becomes unmistakable. The word gives the acts their meaning.

## Forgive

The sharpest line in this draft is also the simplest: you cannot forgive someone by doing something.

Apology can be mimed. A bowed head, a bunch of flowers, a long and awkward silence at the door: these can all say sorry without a syllable. Forgiveness has no such stand-in. Staying in the room is not forgiveness. Resuming normal life is not forgiveness. Those can be tolerance, exhaustion, or avoidance, and the person who wronged you has no way of telling which.

Spoken, the word does something an act cannot. It releases both parties. The one who was wronged puts down the claim they have been holding. The one who did the wronging is told, plainly, that the claim is gone. Neither has to guess, and neither has to keep carrying it.

A hug after a quarrel is ambiguous. It might mean everything is settled, or it might mean nobody wants to talk. The words are not ambiguous. This echoes what we saw with love: the act leaves a question open, and the word closes it.

## Friend, Believe

These two belong together. Both are words that change a relationship, or hand something over, simply by being spoken.

Take "friend." Saying it is a kind of promotion. Two people can spend years in each other's company, sharing jokes and favors, and still be something undefined. Then one of them says the word, and the relationship is no longer the same. Naming changes the thing. [Personal anecdote about the first time someone was called a friend, to be supplied.]

"Believe" works the same way, and it works because it is spoken aloud. Believing someone silently is private and invisible; they cannot lean on it. Said out loud, it becomes something you give them. It is a transfer of trust, made at the moment of speaking, and the listener can hold it from then on.

[One personal line about being told "I believe you," to be supplied.]

In both cases, the word is not a report on something that already happened. It is the event.

## Always

This is where the argument ends. Actions are trapped in the present. Whatever you do, you do now. You can hold someone's hand today, show up this week, keep a promise this year, but each of those is a single moment, and none of them reaches past itself.

Only words reach forward. "Always" is a claim about a time that has not arrived, and an act has no grammar for that. A gesture cannot say "and tomorrow, too." Only the word can stretch the present into a future and bind the speaker to it.

That is also why it is the riskiest word on the list. To say "always" is to promise something you cannot yet know you can deliver. Time will test it, and it may fail the test. The speaker has no guarantee, only the willingness to say it anyway and to be held to it.

Every other word here asks you to be brave in the moment. This one asks you to be brave for as long as you have said you will be.

Gibran once said that words are the cask wherein wine of wisdom is poured and offered to neighbors, not the wine itself. It's a bold statement, but also one which neatly illustrates the importance of what we say, and how we say it. Nothing worth saying can ever be said perfectly, but everything worth saying can be ruined by its mere attempt. The same is true of fiction writing, which is why understanding the power of implication is essential to creating narratives that are as compelling and memorable as possible.

The golden rule to understanding the power of implication, is to avoid saying anything which can be conveyed simply and effectively through actions. That's not to say that spoken lines shouldn't be used at all, but it does mean that one should be wary of using them to convey things that can be conveyed through action. Let's look at the example of love, which is perhaps the most basic, and arguably the most important emotion of all. Saying the words 'I love you' is an easy and powerful sentence, but one which is equally open to misinterpretation as it is to meaning. Actions are much more clear, and they can be much more eloquent in conveying the nature of a character's love than any spoken words.

The power of implication doesn't only apply to positive emotions, it also applies to negative ones, and this can be demonstrated by the example of forgiveness. There's no shortage of films and television shows featuring characters delivering heart-rending apologies to their friends, family and loved ones. However, while these apologies can be deeply moving, they rarely match the raw power of an act of forgiveness which is purely wordless. Two characters hugging each other in the wake of a bitter argument need say nothing to their audience to make them understand the true meaning of their forgiveness.

Another powerful example of the power of implication is provided by the words 'friend' and 'believe'. By applying these terms to someone, we are effectively elevating them to a new level of importance in our lives, and often giving them more power than we had initially intended. However, there's no need to say these words to a character to convey their importance, merely having them perform an act which reveals this is often all that's required to convey the importance of the relationship. The flipside to the word 'believe' is perhaps even more compelling, because it can mean the difference between life and death. When a character says that they believe in someone, they are giving that person a reason to live, and to fight, even when all hope seems lost.

While the power of implication can be applied to broad and abstract concepts like the ones described above, it can also be applied to much simpler ones, and it is here where we find the most compelling examples of all. The reason that implication is so powerful, is because it allows you to present a situation and its consequences in such a way that the audience's mind fills in the gaps for you. When you do this, you are giving the audience a much greater sense of ownership over the story than you would be if you provided them with everything. It also allows you to draw attention to the things you want your audience to notice, and in doing so, you provide them with the opportunity to interpret your creation in a way that feels more personal and satisfying than an explicit telling would.

Rabindranath noted that in the "bypass-banality" era we live in, "the noble words… can no longer be spoken." We're lucky that Seven Words could only have been said by one who "speaks in a language no other can understand". I had begun this piece thinking I'd use it as a platform for a few of my own noble words about writing, but in the windup, I realised that there's only one "noble word" that can only be said now, and it's the one word to which the piece's title refers. It can only be said now because it's the only one that can truly capture life's utter pointlessness, and which is constantly seeking its own justification. What can only be said now is the word "nothing".

## Love

The word "nothing" could only be spoken in these times of utter pointlessness that we live in, where everything seems to have been done and said, and which we are now merely doing and saying again - except for the odd bit of trying to put a new coating on the old, and which we do in the name of progress, but which we all know is nothing but regression. This is the age of the standardised hug, and of the standardised one-size-fits-all statement, and of the standardised smiley face. This is the age of the copy-pastable pithy thought, and of the copy-pastable fake-noble statement. In this age, when the noblest of words have been conveniently discarded, one word that can only be said now is the word "nothing", because it's the only one that can truly capture the utter pointlessness of life. And it can only be said now, because it's the only word that can truly capture the fact that there's nothing more to life than a never-ending quest to prove that life is worth living. The word "nothing" may seem like a word that has no use, but it's the only word that gives meaning to the acts that populate our lives. In an age of pointlessness, "nothing" is the only thing that has value, because without it, there would be nothing at all to do.

The late poet and artist Gibran Khalil Gibran provoked thought, saying "Wisdom is a butterfly, and not a statue." In my thinking, this could be interpreted as meaning that wisdom is something so ethereal and not "touchable" that it cannot be shown in stone, it cannot be displayed as a statue. If wisdom were a statue, it would be a statue of wisdom. We could go to visit the statue of wisdom, but we could never have the real wisdom, only the statue.

The paradoxes of wisdom
I am tempted to think of wisdom as a paradox, or perhaps wisdom and paradox are synonyms. Paradox is a word that intrigues me. In the dictionary, it is defined as "any statement that is seemingly contradictory or opposed to common sense and yet is perhaps true." It would seem to me that wisdom as a concept would need to include the idea of paradox if it is to have any meaning. Wisdom, it seems to me, would have to be a fluid concept, given to constant change and not easily defined by a statue. The statue of wisdom might actually be a symbol of limited wisdom, constricted by its very nature as a statue.

The question of limits
An artistic statue is a fixed object. It is limited by the materials from which it is made, and by the form that has been imposed on the materials. It may be eloquent in its visual impact, but limited in terms of its actions. It cannot move, it cannot speak, it cannot respond to changes in its environment.

## Love

I can think of an example that might illustrate the limits of action as a means of communication. Consider the word love. The idea of love is so important to us that the word cannot be said enough. Yet even the word love is not enough. We need to demonstrate our love for one another. We need to show the actions that are part of love, such as caring, nurturing, giving, and listening. We need to demonstrate our love by hugging and holding, by giving a kiss, or just by sitting quietly together.

The limits of words
There are things I want to say, yet it is not always easy to say them in a way that others will understand. Some things are too important to be left unsaid, yet sometimes I feel that the words are not capable of expressing the ideas. I have often heard it said that "Actions speak louder than words." I would have to agree with that sentiment to a point. I think that actions do speak louder than words, but some things can only be said. There are times when there is no action that will suffice, only words.

The seven words
I think there are some things that can only be said. There is one word that comes to mind right now: Beautiful. I think I will give the other six words as much thought and time as I have with this one, because there are bound to be more than seven words that can only be said.
<end of article>

## Forgive

The word forgive is one that I think has great power. This is one of the words that I think can only be said. It cannot be demonstrated with an action. You can hug someone that you have hurt, and you can ask that person to forgive you, but the forgiveness is only given when the words are said. You can apologize, but an apology is not forgiveness. An apology can open the way for forgiveness, but forgiveness is a personal decision. I have heard people say, "I am sorry," and I have never heard the other person say, "I forgive you." I have thought to myself that the only thing left to say is "I forgive you," but I have never said it. I think I am afraid to say it. Maybe I am afraid to say it because I am afraid I will not mean it, or because I am afraid that the other person will misunderstand and think that it was a sarcastic comment, or because the other person will not take it the right way. Whatever the reason, I have never said it out loud. Maybe the next time I will.

## Friend, Believe

The words friend and believe are two more words that I think can only be said. To make someone your friend, you simply cannot do it through an action. You cannot give someone a gift and make them your friend. Some people think you can, but I don't think so. There are people who have said to me that they consider me to be their friend. Sometimes I know why, and sometimes I don't. We may have worked together for a long time, or we may have shared some laughs, or we may have had great conversations. Whatever the reason, I do not think that we are friends until the words are spoken.

There is one exception to my belief that the word friend can only be spoken. I have seen two young people fall in love, and they become friends automatically. They do not need to say the words, because their actions will say it for them. They will care for one another, nurture one another, give to one another, and listen to one another. They do not need to say the words.
Believe is another word that holds great power. When two people believe in one another, it changes their relationship. It is possible to believe in someone without saying it. Sometimes a look or a gesture will reveal that someone believes in you, but it is only when the words are spoken that it is made clear to the other person. I think that it is in the speaking of the words that one person hands something over to the other person. I believe that my friends believe in me, and I believe that

## Always

There is another word that is very powerful, and I think it can only be said. That word is always. It is the only word in my list that is a negative. I think this word can only be said negatively. There is no other way to say it except to say that you will never do something, or that you will not always be there for someone. Love is an action, but it is also a verb. In the verb form, it is possible to say always. I will always love you.

I think that there are some things in life that we can only say, and that we can never truly demonstrate through actions. The actions speak for themselves, and they are only interpreted by the recipient. Actions are trapped in the present, and they can never reach forward into the future. Words reach forward, and they carry a risk. There is a risk of being misunderstood, and there is a risk of saying something that you do not mean. I think the risk is worth it.
<end of article>

I think that it is in the speaking of the words that one person hands something over to the other person.

The rule is not that they are the most beautiful or useful words, but that they are the words that cannot be replaced by anything else. Love is a word that appears ambiguous because duty, habit and guilt all look like love. Saying it removes the ambiguity. It is a risk to name it because then it can’t hide behind the implication. I keep the word because it allows me to make the actions mean something.
Apology can be mimed with a bowed head. Forgiveness cannot be performed in silence because silence is what resentment looks like. The wrongdoer waits for years for a releasing sentence and the speaker is released too. A hug might mean anything, but ‘I forgive you’ means one thing.
Friend is a word that might be a promotion. Acquainted people become friends when one says ‘you’re my friend,’ because saying it changes the relationship. The first time I was introduced as ‘my friend’ felt large because there was no action that could confer that status. It had to be said.

# Body Language as the Silent Driver of Conversation

You have probably heard that 93 percent of communication is nonverbal. It is one of the most repeated claims in the field, and it is wrong. It comes from Albert Mehrabian's research, which was narrow: it looked at how people judge feelings and attitudes when words and tone of voice or facial expression disagree. It never said that 93 percent of all meaning lives outside the words.

So drop the number. But keep the line that body language matters, because the real finding points at something useful. When what we say and how we say it pull in different directions, listeners trust the how. Body language is not most of the message. It is the silent driver of how the message lands, and of how the conversation feels.

## Two channels

Every conversation runs on two channels at once. One carries content: the facts, the request, the argument. The other carries the relationship: whether you respect the person, whether you are at ease, whether you are with them or against them. Words do most of the work on the first channel. Body language does a great deal on the second, and the second sets the frame for everything that follows.

Consider a mismatch. You tell a colleague, "Sure, I'd love to hear your idea," while glancing at your phone with your arms crossed. The content says yes. The relationship channel says you'd rather be elsewhere, and that is the message they will believe.

Now the mirror. You say the same words, put the phone down, turn toward them and lean in slightly. The channels agree, and the invitation is real.

## Alignment, not performance

The core principle is alignment. Your body should say what you actually mean, not what you wish you meant. This is the strongest idea in the whole subject, and it changes how to think about technique.

Faking fails because incongruence gets detected. A practiced smile over irritation, a staged nod over boredom, an open posture held over resentment: people may not name what is wrong, but they sense the gap between signal and intent, and they trust you less for it. Performance adds a second layer of mismatch on top of the first.

The legitimate kind of adjustment is removing noise. Much of what bodies do is not intent at all: the fidgeting, the glance at the clock, the clenched jaw, the arms folded only because the room is cold. Clearing that away lets your real intent come through undistorted. You are not adding a signal. You are clearing the static.

The limit case follows directly. If you don't mean it, no posture will say it for you. Fix the intent first, or accept that the body will report the truth.

## Where it counts: hard conversations

Hard conversations are where body language does the most work, and the first risk is the least obvious: unintended dominance. Standing while the other person sits, leaning over a desk, or speaking from behind a barrier can make you loom even when your words are gentle. The person hears a threat you never meant to send.

The fix is concrete. Match their level. Sit if they are sitting, angle your chair rather than facing them squarely across a table, and remove the obstacle between you.

Counterintuitively, less eye contact can help with difficult topics. Steady, unbroken eye contact on a painful subject can feel like an interrogation. Looking away at natural moments, at a notepad or the middle distance, gives the other person room to think and to feel without being watched.

Watch your gestures too. Pointing, chopping hands, and sharp jabbing motions escalate tension, because they read as pressure even when the words are calm. Keep your hands open and low.

And authority? It comes from stillness, not from taking up space.

## Calibrate both ways

No rule substitutes for watching the person in front of you. Read their response: if they lean back, go quiet or tighten up, something you are doing is landing badly, whatever the advice says. Adjust, and watch again. Norms vary across cultures, so hold any rule loosely.

Calibration also points inward. Your own body is a signal to yourself. Clenched hands or a held breath can tell you what you are feeling before you have admitted it. Notice it, and ask whether your body and your intent agree. That, in the end, is the whole point: alignment.

The tip on body language comes at the end, a scant paragraph, one that rattled under the gaze of a discerning colleague. “You’re missing the point,” she said. “You’re telling people to fake it, to pretend to be something they’re not. That won’t work.”

She was right. She was also spot-on with her follow-up. “The issue,” she added, “isn’t faking it—it’s alignment.”

That brings us to a myth, one that gets trotted out in the introduction. The claim—Mehrabian’s narrow finding, not the gross 93% oversell—is that most of the meaning comes not from what you say but from how you say it. Once we puncture that fast, we can keep the line for the rest of the piece.

To be clear, we’re only doing one thing here: we’re re-drawing the frame. From here on, everything is about content vs. relationship. We’re not going to elaborate on that split further. Instead, we’re going to illustrate it, one example after another.

The first: a mismatch. In the negative end of the spectrum, you could have a content mismatch. Your words talk about the big picture, but your body language makes the topic seem small. Or you could have a more direct mismatch: your words are about the big picture, but your body language is hard to read. Whatever the specifics, you’re giving off mixed signals, and that’s a problem.

And what’s the solution? We’ve got to align ourselves. The conversation is a joint effort, and both parties need to dial into that.

The point here is that the content mismatch is like a noisy signal. It’s the opposite of alignment. The other party can’t hear what you’re saying, and if you want to fix that, you’ve got to remove the noise. There’s nothing wrong with adjusting your body language, but you’ve got to be doing it for the right reason. If you’re feeling relaxed and you push your body language to a more tense state, that’s not an adjustment—that’s a performance. And people will see through it.

So we want to cut the noise. The way to do that is to dial into your intent. In conversations, the more clear your intent, the more aligned your body language will be to it.

The key here is that the intent doesn’t have to be obvious. If your intent is to go to war, you’re going to have a pretty big mismatch with your body language. But that’s the opposite of alignment. Instead, take a look at your most recent hard conversation. Were you trying to lead, or were you trying to avoid? Did your body language reflect that intent?

Let’s bring in an example here, one that’s got both kinds of mismatch: the content mismatch and the relationship mismatch.

You’re giving a presentation. It’s your second time through, but you’re not sure if you’re getting through to the team. You’re opening your eyes wide and dropping your hands to your sides. That should be big picture, but it’s coming across as small.

The answer: pay attention to how he’s responding to your questions. If he’s leaning in, he’s indicating interest. In that case, you can dial down the eye contact. After all, this is a hard conversation, and if he’s leaning in, you can give him more space. You don’t have to avoid his gaze. But you can dial it down.

Now bring this back to yourself: pay attention to your own body language. It’s a signal to yourself, a way to gauge your own intent. If you’re leaning back, take that as a signal that you’re avoiding the topic. Get your posture back on track, and you’ll be well on your way.

That’s the kernel, and it’s the thesis. The rest of the article is a series of examples that illustrate the point. There are some core principles that we weave through, and we call them out explicitly:

1. Alignment, not performance.
2. Where it counts: hard conversations.
3. Calibrate both ways.

The first is the core principle, and it’s the strongest idea in the piece, so it gets the most room. The second is crucial, so we want to give it its due. And the third comes at the end: a concrete takeaway for the reader. It ties the thesis back into the frame that we opened with, and it closes out the piece.

That’s the piece. And that’s the method: take a kernel, tie it to the frame, and expand it one example at a time.

This is not always a bad thing; when we disengage with our mouths and engage with our bodies, we can learn things about ourselves.

In conversation, we speak through two channels: one that conveys content, and the other that conveys relationship. Relationship relates to how much we like and respect the other person - or not. The content channel is more or less the conscious stream of words and concepts, while the relationship channel operates on a more unconscious level, and it's communicated largely through body language.

The root problem is that we think we need to use our bodies to achieve some specific effect - to perform, in other words. And when we try to do that, we end up looking fake. The real key, which is much harder to achieve, is to aim for alignment. Alignment means removing the barriers between you and the other person, so that the two of you can talk on the same wavelength, instead of constantly having to translate for each other. Fake signals get detected
The reason we look fake when we try to use our bodies to create a specific effect is that it's very hard to fool the other person when we're not expressing our real feelings and attitudes. The human brain is exquisitely tuned to detect incongruence, so when we try to act in a way that doesn't align with our real feelings, the other person will usually sense the inconsistency. Legitimate adjustments
The trick is to not try to "perform" with your body, as if you were staging a play. Instead, aim to remove barriers that get in the way of clear communication. For example, if you've got a habit of crossing your arms over your chest, take care to uncross your arms before you begin speaking, so that you won't give the other person the sense that you're shutting them out.

This principle is especially important in hard conversations. No gestures, please
Another thing that can get in the way of communication is too much gesturing. This is a mistake that many people make when they're trying to communicate a difficult message; they think that if they get more animated, the other person will be more engaged. Too many gestures can make the other person feel unsettled, and gestures can also take away from your message of authority and gravitas, which comes from stillness.

# GDP Measures Output, Not Well-Being

Gross domestic product tells us how much an economy produces. It was never built to tell us how well people live, and treating it as if it did produces errors that are easy to make and hard to see. Output can rise while most households gain nothing. It can be large in a country where each person has little. It can leave out work that sustains whole societies, and it can count destruction as progress. Each of these is a gap between what GDP records and what well-being requires, and each deserves a closer look.

## Divide by people first

Total output says little about individual lives until it is divided by the number of people who share it. Consider two countries. Country A produces four times as much as Country B, yet its output per head is one fifth as large. Ranking by total output puts A far ahead. Ranking by output per head reverses the order, and the second ranking is the one closer to ordinary living standards.

The sharpest consequence concerns growth. An economy can post rising GDP while its people grow worse off. If population increases faster than output, the total climbs and output per head falls. Headline growth then masks decline. The figure that gets reported and celebrated moves up while the average person's share moves down. A reader who sees a growth rate without the population trend behind it can be misled about the direction of change, not merely its size. This is why per capita figures should be the default, and why a total deserves suspicion when it appears alone.

Comparisons across countries should also adjust for purchasing power parity, which corrects for the different price levels in each place, since the same income buys different amounts in different countries.

## Averages hide who gets it

Even output per head describes a mean, and a mean says nothing about distribution. Two countries can have identical output per head and offer their citizens very different lives. Picture one where gains are spread widely and a typical family shares in them. Picture another where a small group captures most of the output, so a typical family has far less than the average suggests. The statistic is the same, but the lives are not.

The bite comes when growth is set against the median. GDP per capita can rise year after year while the income of the median person stays flat or falls, because the gains go to people already above it. The average improves, and the person in the middle sees nothing. Growth reported as a national success then describes the experience of a minority. Judging whether growth reaches ordinary households requires a measure of the middle and the spread, which GDP does not supply.

## Unrecorded work

GDP captures what is traded and measured, so it misses a large amount of productive activity. Work in the informal economy and unpaid work both create value that people depend on, yet neither appears in the accounts. What matters is the consequence, not the categories.

That consequence is a skew in comparisons. A country where much production happens outside recorded markets will look poorer than the work its people actually do would warrant. One where the same tasks are bought and sold will look richer for doing the same things. The distortion falls hardest on developing economies, where more of this activity goes unrecorded. Differences in GDP between countries then partly reflect how much activity gets recorded rather than how much gets done.

## Damage counted as gain

GDP adds up output but never subtracts the costs of producing it. Pollution shows the problem. The activity that generates it adds to output, while the harm it does never enters the ledger as a loss. An economy can degrade its surroundings and report only the gain.

The perverse case is disaster cleanup. Spending to clear debris and rebuild is activity, so it raises GDP, even though the disaster left people poorer. What was destroyed goes unrecorded as a loss, while the spending to repair it is counted as a gain.

The root cause is how the measure is built. GDP is assembled from market transactions. It records what is bought and sold at the price paid. Whatever is not exchanged is invisible, and whatever is exchanged counts as positive, whether it makes people better off or merely restores what they had. The measure has no way to tell spending that creates from spending that repairs.

Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is a key indicator used in measuring the economy’s health. GDP is the monetary value of all final goods and services produced within a country’s borders during a specific period of time. However, this measurement does not take into account important factors like leisure, life expectancy, or happiness. GDP is not intended to measure well-being, and it is often misinterpreted as a measure of well-being. The human toll of rising inequality, soaring health care and education costs, and rising unemployment are ignored in the GDP measure. In contrast, the Genuine Progress Indicator (GPI) tries to take into account factors not measured by GDP, like the negative environmental impacts of economic activity.

GDP per capita tells us little about well-being because it does not take into account the distribution of income and/or wealth in a country. It also fails to take into account inequality within a country, and ignores the value of unpaid work. The GPI, on the other hand, accounts for changes in income distribution within a country and attempts to quantify the value of unpaid work such as housework and volunteering.

There are other important factors that are not included in the GDP measure. These include the costs of natural resource depletion and pollution. These costs are not included in the GDP measure because they are not market transactions. If a company pollutes a river, for example, the cost of cleaning up the pollution is included in the GDP measure, but the costs of the pollution itself are not. The GPI measures these costs and subtracts them from the GDP measure.

The GPI is an imperfect measure, but it is a more comprehensive measure than the GDP. By accounting for factors that are not included in the GDP measure, the GPI gives us a more complete picture of a country’s well-being. While the GDP measure may have been useful in the past, it is clear that we need to move beyond it and develop more comprehensive measures of well-being.

GDP Measures Output, Not Well-Being
A GDP measurement, while useful as an indicator of economic output, fails to gauge the well-being of a nation's citizens.

## Divide by people first

A country with four times the population of another, having four times the output, may have a fifth of the output per person of the less populous country. You can see the point when it is better to divide output by people first, and then compare countries. The sharper point is that a country's growth can mask a decline in well-being, so give this measurement its proper place.

## Averages hide who gets it

The same per capita output may give different lives to people. Let's consider a concrete case where a country's output grows from $20,000 to $30,000 per person per year. This is a 50% increase. However, if we look at median income, that may have decreased, due to a reduction in the middle of the distribution, with an upward movement of the poor and a lot more growth by the wealthy. The bite is that 20% may have been added to the wealth of 2% of the people, but 2% is not the median. The median is 50% of the distribution, so the bite is that the median person has $19,000, at most, while the median person had $20,000 before. In this case, the median person is actually worse off, even though the country's output has grown.

## Unrecorded work

Unrecorded work and unpaid work can skew comparisons, especially for developing economies. The informal economy - cash transactions, ranging from farming to haircuts to laundering money - represents a significant percentage of economic output in developing economies, yet this output is generally not included in national accounts. As well, much of the work that people perform around the world is unpaid, such as raising children, maintaining households, and caring for elderly parents. These efforts represent real costs and should be factored into a proper assessment of well-being.

## Damage counted as gain

Pollution contributes to economic output, while the costs of environmental degradation are never subtracted. One perverse example is that the cleanup of a disaster, whether natural or man-made, will add to a nation's GDP. This perverse accounting stems from the very root of GDP, built as it is from market transactions. Gross domestic product is the total of goods and services bought and sold within a country. It includes all market transactions, regardless of their social utility or environmental impact. Anything that is bought and sold is counted as a benefit, including the arms trade, drugs, and the sale of polluting, global-warming, or genetically engineered products.

Quick Review
The key takeaway is that GDP is an excellent measure of total market output but a poor stand-alone measure of economic well-being. Real GDP per capita is preferable for comparing living standards but should be interpreted with caution.
Limitation 1: Population Differences
If A has four times the total output of B, then per person, A has a GDP of $10,000 and B has a GDP of $50,000. The average resident of B has far more goods and services available to them.
This is why GDP per capita is a better measure. If real GDP grows 3 percent but the population increases 4 percent, output per person falls. On average, living standards are likely declining.
In addition, adjustments for purchasing power parity (PPP) are often used to take into account differences in price levels across countries.
Limitation 2: Income Inequality
Identical GDP per capita can mean very different living conditions. Two countries can have the same GDP per capita but very different income distributions. For example, if the top 1 percent of households earns half of all income, the per capita GDP can look healthy, but the typical household may struggle. Rising GDP does not guarantee that the gains will be shared with everyone. Growth can concentrate among high earners while median incomes stagnate.
Limitation 3: Shadow Economy
Not only does GDP exclude non-market production, but it also excludes unpaid work such as housework, childcare, and volunteer work. Even though this work has a real value, it is not a market transaction and so is not included. The size of the shadow economy varies widely. In some developing countries, informal economic activity makes up a large share of output. Official GDP can substantially understate activity and make cross-country comparisons less accurate.
Limitation 4: Environmental Costs
A polluting factory adds to GDP, but the lost water quality and increased health care costs are not subtracted. The costs of disaster cleanup can increase GDP since the spending on repair and remediation counts as production. This is related to the concept of negative externalities – costs imposed on third parties that are not reflected in market prices. Since GDP is built from market transactions, it does not capture them. A country can have strong growth while at the same time degrading the natural capital future generations need.
The use of GDP as a measure of economic well-being is not without its limitations. These include differences in population, income inequality, the shadow economy, and environmental costs.

The key takeaway is that while GDP is an excellent measure of total market output, it is a poor stand-alone measure of well-being. Real GDP per capita is preferred when comparing living standards, but should be interpreted with caution.
If country A has four times the total output of country B, then on a per person basis A has a GDP of $10,000 while B has a GDP of $50,000. Thus, on average, a person in country B has far more goods and services than a person in country A.
If real GDP grows by 3 percent but the population grows by 4 percent, then output per person falls. Given this, we would expect that on average living standards are declining.
In many cases, PPP adjustments are used to account for price-level differences across countries.
A country with identical GDP per capita could still have very different living conditions if the income distribution is very broad (i.e., there are large differences between the highest and lowest incomes) or concentrated (i.e., there is not a lot of difference between the highest and lowest incomes).
For example, if the top 1 percent of households in a country earn half of all income, then the per capita income may look healthy, but the typical household in that country may struggle. Furthermore, just because GDP is rising does not mean that everyone is experiencing gains; GDP growth can concentrate among high earners while median incomes remain stagnant.
Non-market production is also excluded, such as unpaid housework, childcare, and volunteer work. Although this activity has real value, it does not take place through a market transaction. The size of the shadow economy varies widely across countries. In some developing countries, informal economic activity may represent a large share of output, so official GDP figures can substantially understate economic activity and make cross-country comparisons less accurate.
When a polluting factory is built, this activity increases GDP. However, the lost water quality and associated health costs are not subtracted. Similarly, if a disaster occurs and cleanup increases GDP because repair/remediation spending is counted as production, then this is also an example of GDP not accurately reflecting well-being. The link between this issue and negative externalities is that costs that impact third parties are not captured in market prices. Because GDP is built from market transactions, these negative externalities are missed. This means that a country can post strong economic growth while degrading its natural capital that future generations will need.

# Kelp Pills Can Disrupt the Thyroid They Promise to Help

Kelp supplements are marketed as support for the thyroid. They can also disrupt it. The irony is hard to miss: a product sold to protect a gland can be the thing that throws it off. Kelp reaches consumers as pills and in other supplement forms, and the pills are where the trouble concentrates.

## A narrow safe window

The amount an adult needs is tiny. The recommended ceilings are low, and they differ by jurisdiction, so even the official line on "too much" depends on where you live.

The thyroid has a safety brake that usually works. When intake runs high, the gland tends to protect itself. Sometimes the brake fails, and then excess intake disrupts the gland instead of being absorbed harmlessly.

The harm runs in both directions. Too much of the nutrient can push thyroid function off course one way or the other, so the risk is not limited to a single kind of patient. Some people are more exposed than others, and the brake is least reliable in exactly those people.

The effects can also reach a second person. Newborns can be exposed through the mother, so a supplement one adult takes can affect an infant who never chose it.

## Why supplements are the problem

The number that does the work is the gap between what the body needs and what a supplement can deliver. Need is tiny and ceilings are low, so a single pill can overshoot both. That is the core problem.

Labels do not close the gap, because they are unreliable. What is printed on the bottle may not match what is inside, so a careful reader can still be wrong about the dose.

Concentration and stacking compound the problem. A concentrated product is risky on its own. Add a second supplement, or a few, and the total becomes invisible. No single label shows the sum, and the person swallowing it all may never add it up.

The sharpest point is about who buys these products. Marketing selects for the vulnerable. A product pitched at thyroid trouble reaches people who are already worried about their thyroid, which means it reaches the people least able to absorb a mistake. The audience is not a random cross-section of the public. It is the group the pitch is built to attract, and it is the group with the most to lose if the brake fails. The promise of help is the mechanism that delivers the product to those it can hurt most. The risk is not spread evenly and then occasionally concentrated by bad luck. The sales pitch concentrates it on purpose, or at least by design.

This is not only theory. There is evidence of real harm.

One check is concrete. Look at the label and add up the amount from every supplement you take, not just the kelp. If you cannot find or trust the number, treat that as the answer.

## The Japan objection

The strongest objection comes from Japan. Intake there is far above Western limits, and there is no crisis. If high intake were dangerous, the argument goes, Japan would show it.

The key contrast is adaptation versus sudden start. A population that has eaten a certain way for generations has adapted. Someone who starts a concentrated pill tomorrow has not. The brake may hold for the first and fail for the second.

The comparison also breaks down on the details. Species differ, preparation differs, and day-to-day intake swings. Food is not a pill. Kelp eaten as part of meals, prepared in a particular way, varies from one day to the next, while a pill delivers the same concentrated dose every time. The Japanese diet and the supplement aisle are not the same exposure, even when both involve kelp.

Even Japan has documented cases. A high-intake country with no crisis still has people who were harmed, which shows the window is narrow there too. Adaptation lowers the risk without removing it. The objection, taken seriously, supports the case against the pills rather than undermining it.

Kelp pills are widely marketed as a natural, no-risk thyroid support supplement. Manufacturers assure consumers that products are safe because they contain only natural ingredients and are sold as dietary supplements. Yet natural ingredients can still pose health risks, and the thyroid is one of the body systems most vulnerable to the potential harms of natural supplements.

The thyroid has two basic functions: to increase the body's metabolic rate when necessary, and to maintain metabolic rate to keep hormone levels balanced. It regulates the body's metabolism, creating and releasing hormones that maintain the body's heart rate, digestion, muscle control, brain development, and body temperature.

A healthy thyroid gland produces two hormones: T3 (triiodothyronine) and T4 (thyroxine), which regulate the rate at which the body produces energy. The thyroid gland itself is controlled by two other hormones, TRH (thyrotropin-releasing hormone) and TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone). When levels of T3 and T4 are too low, the pituitary gland releases TSH, prompting the thyroid to increase production; when levels are too high, the pituitary gland reduces TSH, signaling the thyroid to slow down. In other words, it's a system of checks and balances. When it's working properly, the thyroid maintains a healthy metabolism, and the body functions smoothly.

Kelp can disrupt this system because it contains high levels of iodine and other thyroid-affecting compounds. While kelp can also contain other nutrients and minerals, these are often present in trace amounts. In essence, the nutrient value of kelp doesn't merit the risks. Supplements containing kelp (or marketed as kelp) include kelp granules, ground kelp, bladderwrack, fucus, and other seaweed preparations.

The human body does need iodine to maintain its metabolic rate and produce thyroid hormones. In fact, iodine is so critical to thyroid function that it's considered an "essential" nutrient. But the body only needs trace amounts of iodine each day, usually about 150 micrograms; this is typically found in fruits, vegetables, dairy products, meat, poultry, fish, and eggs.

The amount of iodine in kelp supplements varies widely from product to product, and iodine can be difficult to measure. In some studies, kelp supplements contained only trace amounts, but other studies found the iodine content to be much higher. One study found that 11.7% of kelp supplements contained more than 150 micrograms of iodine per tablet, and that 26.8% contained more than 500 micrograms. Even trace amounts of iodine can be harmful if they're not needed, and iodine levels above 500 micrograms can cause an overdose.

Because the amount of iodine is unknown, it's difficult to determine what kelp dose might be safe. In fact, the Food and Drug Administration has not approved any claim that a kelp-based supplement is beneficial, or even safe. There are no established guidelines for safe kelp intake, and most supplements are not standardized. In fact, most bottles of kelp supplements sold in the United States do not even list the amount of iodine contained in each tablet.

Without that information, it's difficult to determine whether kelp pills are safe, especially if a product does contain high levels of iodine. When healthy individuals take kelp, thyroid hormone levels might increase or decrease. If the thyroid produces too much hormone, a condition known as hyperthyroidism, heart rate might increase, body temperature might rise, and the person might experience anxiety, insomnia, and hair loss. Conversely, if the thyroid produces too little hormone, a condition known as hypothyoneism, the body might be slow to react, the person might lose weight and feel cold, and the mind might become sluggish.

The potential risks of kelp supplements are not limited to overdose, however. In one study, researchers found that one-third of kelp supplements contained arsenic, a toxic substance that can be harmful at low levels. Children who take kelp supplements might be exposed to heavy metals like arsenic, and pregnant and breastfeeding women who take the supplements might expose their children to high levels of these metals. Kelp supplements might also contain high levels of bromide, which can interfere with iodine and cause goiter, or an enlargement of the thyroid gland. Kelp supplements might also contain lead, radionuclides, cadmium, mercury, or other metals that can be toxic.

Kelp supplements might also be dangerous for people with thyroid disorders. Patients who take thyroid medication might get too much medication if they also take kelp supplements, because the iodine in kelp can alter the amount of medication needed. And while iodine is often used to treat thyroid disorders, too much iodine can actually worsen the disorder. Patients with hypothyroidism, for example, might experience an increase in their symptoms if they take kelp supplements.

While healthy individuals who take kelp supplements are unlikely to experience side effects, iodine toxicity can be dangerous. In very severe cases, hypothyroidism can lead to a coma or death. And kelp supplements, unfortunately, tend to target consumers who are concerned about their thyroid health and who might be more at risk for problems. In essence, the marketing of kelp supplements selects for the vulnerable.

Yet the risks of kelp supplements do not concern consumers as much as they might think. In one study, researchers found that 7.4% of respondents reported taking a supplement with iodine in the past year, but only 2.9% knew that kelp supplements can be unsafe. When consumers do know about the risks, they often assume the products are safe because they're natural and therefore unlikely to cause harm.

Kelp supplements are marketed as a natural cure for thyroid problems. While it's true that the thyroid needs iodine to produce hormones, it's also true that too much iodine can disrupt the thyroid. In fact, the thyroid can only absorb so much iodine, and once that limit is reached, the thyroid can become inflamed or enlarged. The body also has a safety mechanism that limits the amount of iodine absorbed, but this mechanism can fail under some circumstances.

The thyroid has a narrow safety window. When it receives just the right amount of iodine, it functions properly and produces the hormones needed to maintain the body's metabolism. But when the thyroid receives too much iodine, it might increase hormone production. When it receives too little iodine, it might decrease hormone production. And when it gets too much iodine at once, it might shut down production entirely.

Kelp supplements may be marketed as natural, but that doesn't mean they're safe. In fact, while these products can disrupt the delicate balance of the body's metabolic rate, they can also disrupt the body's natural defense against iodine overdose. Consumers concerned about thyroid health should speak with a clinician, but they should also proceed with caution if they're considering a kelp supplement.
