Kelp Pills Can Disrupt the Thyroid
Ironic isn't it? Promoted as a thyroid health treatment, but actually can disrupt the thyroid. This is true with Kelp Pills. They do contain iodine, an element necessary for normal thyroid function. However, when iodine is lacking, the thyroid gland enlarges to compensate and form a goiter. In this condition, iodine increases the size of goiters. Taken in excess, iodine is also a detriment to health. Although iodine deficiency is now uncommon, the fact remains that kelp pills can disrupt the thyroid.

## A narrow safe window

The need for iodine is tiny. Adults are advised to get about 150 micrograms a day. For pregnant women, it's 220 micrograms. And for those who breastfeed, the recommended dosage goes up to 290 micrograms. All of this iodine is usually found in the diet, and so a supplement is not necessary. These are upper limits. Excessive amounts of iodine can also be harmful. Too much iodine can disrupt hormone action, and this is why. The thyroid gland produces hormones that regulate how quickly the body burns calories and uses energy. Iodine regulates this function, and there is a safety brake. But this brake sometimes doesn't work.

## Why supplements are the problem

The problem is that when iodine is taken as a supplement, the thyroid gland cannot tell how much iodine is normal and how much is too much. The available iodine is regulated by the pituitary gland, but this organ cannot distinguish between iodine from seaweed pills and iodine already in the diet. So it's easy to take too much. And iodine excess is hard to detect, since you cannot see any signs. In fact, a goiter might form, but this is hard to see. The only effective way to check for an iodine toxicity is to test the blood. Kelp pills are marketed as a thyroid health supplement, but they can disrupt the thyroid.

## The Japan objection

You might object that there is no epidemic of iodine toxicity in Japan, where the consumption of seaweed is at higher levels than in the west. However, this objection doesn't hold up. The Japanese eat seaweed regularly, but they prepare it in different ways. The preparation reduces the iodine content, and this lowers the intake to safe levels. And Japanese consumption fluctuates over time, as traditional foods give way to modern foods. There are documented cases of Japanese iodine poisoning. This can happen suddenly, and if it does, then there is no time to adapt. The sharp contrast is between a gradual adaptation to gradual changes in iodine levels, and the sharp spike of a sudden overdose. This is why seaweed consumption is safe in Japan but not in the west.

sec2.text:
Kelp Pills Can Disrupt the Thyroid
I recently talked to a woman about hypothyroidism, and she mentioned she was taking kelp pills to help her thyroid. Just saying that made me squirm in my chair, because I know that kelp supplements can disrupt the thyroid. People take kelp supplements because kelp naturally contains iodine, and the thyroid needs iodine to produce its hormones. But iodine in excess disrupts the thyroid. Too much can also cause a goiter.

## A narrow safe window

The body needs very little iodine. Adults can manage with 150 micrograms or less. That's about the amount in one gram of potato chips, or a half-ounce glass of whole milk. Upper limits for iodine are also low, and they differ somewhat by jurisdiction. The Upper limit in the United States, for example, is 1,600 micrograms for adults. That's a tiny window between too little and too much iodine. The body's mechanism to prevent iodine toxicity works very well, but sometimes it fails. When that happens, a number of thyroid-related problems can result.

Iodine harms
Excess iodine can both suppress and activate the thyroid gland, and other problems can occur as well. These include goiter, thyroiditis, and thyroid cancer, and problems from skin to the nervous system. More generally, excess iodine can cause weakness, fatigue, nausea, and diarrhea, and also skin rash, acne, and increased sweating. The whole body suffers.

## Why supplements are the problem

The core problem is that supplement labels do not accurately report the amounts of iodine in the supplements. They are so unreliable that even the scientific journal article I first read on this subject recommended that consumers should not take kelp supplements. It can be difficult to know how much iodine is in a supplement, because iodine comes in a variety of forms. A particular product formulation may also add up to more than what is indicated on the label, because it can be in multiple ingredients. The amount of iodine in a single day's dose of kelp may be very high. And most people do not know this.

Kelp supplements attractive to vulnerable
Marketing for kelp supplements usually targets the vulnerable. They are sold as a cure for hypothyolroidism, but they are not a replacement for your thyroid medication. The supplements are also marketed for weight loss, for example. Since the iodine content is unreliable, the supplements can be a problem for a person who is already at risk, because they are iodine-sensitive. It is especially important for pregnant women to avoid the supplements, because their baby's thyroid is still developing.

Evidence of harm
The scientific evidence on this subject is divided. It appears that the body can usually protect itself, but in some cases it cannot. The problem is that when the protection mechanism fails, a number of thyroid-related problems can result. There is also evidence of harm from excess iodine, although it is not conclusively proven. There are many more studies than might be expected, because the topic has been controversial for decades. Most doctors caution against the supplements, and the government and many organizations warn against them.

Check total from all sources
The amounts of iodine in supplements can be surprising. But it is also important to check total iodine intake from all sources. This includes foods, medicines, and even food-packaging materials. You can check your intake at the website www.foodfacts.info. For example, you can check your total iodine intake for the day, in micrograms, by adding up the amounts in a few rows. But this does not mean you should absolutely avoid iodine. The body needs iodine. The safest approach is to get your daily amount of iodine from a variety of foods.

## The Japan objection

You may have heard that the Japanese diet includes far more iodine than Western limits, yet they do not have a thyroid epidemic. This is because the amounts are built into their diet. They don't dump it into their bodies in a pill and so the body can adapt. This does not mean that there is no risk at all. Even in Japan, there are documented cases of thyroid dysfunction. The Japanese diet includes more iodine than Western diets. But the increase in iodine in the Japanese diet has occurred over the course of many years. For example, the amount of iodine in seaweed has been increasing over the centuries. On the other hand, supplement intake occurs suddenly, and in large amounts.

Iodine in the diet
If you eat a variety of foods, your risk from iodine is likely to be low. But it can still add up. For example, the maximum daily amount of iodine in foods is listed as 1,600 micrograms in the United States. How can this amount be determined, since different foods contain different amounts? One researcher has demonstrated that you can eat all of your iodine in one meal. But in the diet, you are very unlikely to eat only iodine-rich foods, such as seaweed. So your total intake is likely to be less than the maximum. And your body is already adapted to gradual increases in intake.

lora13.text:
Seaweed Supplements: Iodine Risks and Microalgae Promise
The wrong form and dose can push iodine levels high enough to disrupt the thyroid gland that the supplement is marketed to help. Sold as dried snacks, powdered “sea greens,” and kelp tablets and capsules, seaweed supplements promise support for the thyroid, detox, and metabolic balance.
Why Iodine Matters, and Why More Isn’t Better
Our bodies only need tiny amounts of iodine, ranging from 150 micrograms (µg) per day for adults to 220 µg during pregnancy and 290 µg during breastfeeding. Upper limits on iodine intake are also modest, with the US tolerable upper intake set at 1,100 µg per day and European authorities recommending a lower limit of 600 µg per day. Our thyroid glands have a built-in brake that slows production of thyroid hormones during periods of high iodine intake, the Wolff–Chaikoff effect. Most healthy people adapt and return to normal levels, but in others, this brake fails or overcorrects. Excess iodine can trigger hypothyroidism, especially with autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashimoto’s disease), or hyperthyroidism (Jod-Basedow phenomenon), more likely with nodular goiter or long-standing iodine deficiency. Iodine excess during pregnancy or breastfeeding can lead to newborn thyroid problems.
The Problem With Seaweed Supplements
One gram of dried kombu can contain over a thousand micrograms of iodine, with some samples containing several times that amount, so even a small pinch can exceed a day’s upper limit for iodine. Here are four things to consider:
1. Iodine is highly variable, differing by species, harvest location, season, and processing. Tests of kelp products repeatedly find levels substantially different from what’s stated on the labels, sometimes by large margins.
2. Powdered and tablet forms make it easy to consume large amounts of dried seaweed without realizing it.
3. People may stack a kelp capsule with a “thyroid support” blend, an iodine multivitamin, and iodized salt, adding up to a total iodine intake that no one ever adds up.
4. Products that target fatigue, weight loss, and “sluggish thyroid” tend to attract people most likely to have conditions that iodine excess worsens. Many case reports link seaweed supplements and seaweed products to thyroid dysfunction in adults and in infants exposed to iodine through supplements during pregnancy or breast milk.
Be wary of supplements that don’t state iodine content per serving in micrograms.
But Doesn’t Japan Eat a Lot of Seaweed?
Japan has one of the world’s highest intakes of iodine, mostly from seaweed. Estimates vary widely, with many ranging from one to several milligrams per day, well above upper limits for iodine in Western countries. Yet Japan has no thyroid crisis.
This may be because:
- People who’ve been exposed to iodine from seaweed throughout their lives may have better-regulating thyroids than those who suddenly start a concentrated iodine supplement.
- Iodine comes from food, not pills, in meals with varied types and amounts of seaweed. Nori and wakame, for example, contain much less iodine than kombu.
- Iodine from seaweed is prepared in meals, not in pill form, and eaten with a variety of types and amounts of seaweed. Kombu is used for dashi broth, then either discarded or eaten in small amounts. Soaking and boiling seaweed removes a substantial share of iodine, though some does get into the broth.
- Iodine intake swings day to day, not in a steady, supplement-like dose.
Japan’s record is not spotless. Iodine-related hypothyroidism has been documented, especially in heavy consumers of kombu. Clinicians often advise limiting seaweed intake in certain thyroid conditions.
Japan’s experience shows that high iodine intake can be tolerated in context. It doesn’t demonstrate that a concentrated kelp capsule is harmless for an adult raised on a low-iodine diet.

Wrong Form and Dose Can Push Iodine High Enough to Disrupt the Thyroid It's Marketed to Help
Seaweed supplements can be sold as dried snacks, powdered "sea greens," kelp tablets, or capsules, and they're sometimes marketed as ways to support the thyroid, detox the body, and achieve metabolic balance.
Iodine is an essential nutrient our bodies need in tiny amounts: adults about 150 micrograms (µg) per day, pregnant women about 220 µg, and breastfeeding women about 290 µg. Our upper limits for iodine are modest, too: in the United States, adults can safely ingest up to 1,100 µg per day, but European authorities set a lower limit of 600 µg per day.
The Wolff–Chaikoff effect is the thyroid's built-in brake, a temporary slowing of hormone production during surges of iodine intake. Most healthy people can adapt and return to normal, but in others, the brake fails or overcorrects. Excess iodine can trigger hypothyroidism, especially when coupled with autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashimoto's), or hyperthyroidism (the Jod-Basedow phenomenon), which is likelier in people with nodular goiter or long-standing iodine deficiency. Excess iodine can also trigger newborn thyroid problems when mothers take high-iodine supplements during pregnancy or breastfeeding.
Here's the problem with seaweed supplements:
1. They contain highly variable amounts of iodine. One gram of dried kombu, for example, can contain more than a thousand µg of iodine, and some samples contain several times that much. A small pinch of seaweed can contain more than an adult's upper limit for iodine intake for the day.
2. They're in powder and tablet form, making it easy to consume large amounts of dried seaweed unnoticed.
3. They can be taken in combination with a kelp capsule, a "thyroid support" supplement, an iodine-containing multivitamin, and iodized salt. The total amount of iodine consumed is never added up.
4. Products marketed for fatigue, weight loss, and "sluggish thyroid" will attract people most likely to have conditions that excess iodine worsens.
There are many case reports of thyroid dysfunction tied to kelp supplements and seaweed products, both in adults and in infants exposed to high iodine intake in utero or via breast milk. Be wary of products that don't state the iodine content per serving in micrograms.
But doesn't Japan eat seaweed?
Japan has one of the highest iodine intakes in the world, mostly from seaweed, and estimates of iodine intake there vary widely, from one to several milligrams (mg) per day, well above Western upper limits for iodine intake. But there's no thyroid crisis in Japan.
1. People have adapted to this iodine intake throughout their lifetimes. The thyroids of people exposed to iodine from childhood might regulate better than those that suddenly start receiving a concentrated iodine supplement.
2. People get their iodine from food, not pills. When seaweed is eaten as part of a meal, it's a varied amount and type of seaweed, and nori and wakame contain much less iodine than kombu.
3. It's prepared differently. Kombu is used to make dashi broth, which is then discarded or eaten in small amounts, and soaking and boiling seaweed removes a substantial share of the iodine, though some does end up in the broth.
4. It's consumed in a variable way. The intake varies day to day, not in a steady, high supplement-like dose.
Japan's record isn't spotless: iodine-related hypothyroidism has been documented in Japan, especially in heavy consumers of kombu, and clinicians often advise people with certain thyroid conditions to limit their seaweed intake.
Our tradition of high iodine intake shows that it can be tolerated in the right context. But it doesn't show that taking a concentrated kelp capsule is harmless for an adult who's been raised on a low-iodine diet.
(If you're not sure how much iodine you're getting from seaweed and other foods, I recommend you calculate your total daily iodine intake. See "What's Your Iodine Intake?" in the references.)

Thanks for reading, everyone. Have a great day!
Mark Sisson

# Bubbles: What Makes Some Burst Harder and Heal Slower

A bubble is a stretch in which the price of an asset is driven by what people expect it to fetch later, not by what the asset produces. The mechanism is a self-fulfilling expectation. Buyers expect prices to rise, so they buy, and their buying makes prices rise, which confirms the expectation and draws in more buyers.

The burst comes when the buyers are exhausted. Nobody is left to pay a higher price, and the expectation that held everything up gives way. But the burst itself is not what matters most. What matters is what decides how bad it gets, and that is the question this piece follows.

## Debt turns a crash into a crisis

Leverage is the multiplier. A crash in which people lose only their own savings hurts, but it stays contained. A crash in which people borrowed to buy becomes something worse, because borrowed money has to be repaid whatever the asset is now worth.

The spiral runs in a clear order. Borrowers default. Lenders, now exposed to losses, retreat and stop lending. Those who still hold debt are forced to sell, and their forced selling pushes prices down further, which creates more defaults. Each step feeds the next.

It usually starts with cheap money flowing into assets. Easy borrowing pushes prices up, rising prices make the assets look safe to borrow against, and that invites more borrowing. The boom feeds itself on the way up, and the same loop runs in reverse on the way down.

The 2008 crisis shows the whole chain in a single case. Housing and credit were not two separate stories but one. Cheap money poured into housing, and when housing fell, the losses did not stay there. They moved into the financial institutions that had lent against it. That is contagion: trouble in one market spreading through the balance sheets that connected it to everything else.

Contagion also reaches innocent bystanders. People and businesses that never speculated on housing found credit harder to get once lenders pulled back. A crash that begins among borrowers and lenders ends up costing people who had no part in the bubble.

## Recovery is measured in decades

The dot-com bubble was built on valuations with nothing underneath. Prices reflected hope about what companies might become, not anything the companies were producing. When the buyers ran out, those prices had nothing to rest on, and they fell hard.

The fall was severe, but the more striking number is the time it took to recover. It took fifteen years for the market to get back to where it had been. A whole working career's worth of patience was needed just to break even for those who bought at the top.

Japan is the extreme case, because the bubble was not confined to one sector. It was an entire economy. When everything is priced on expectation, and the debt behind it is large, there is no healthy part left to pull the rest back up.

The number to remember is thirty. Japan's recovery has been counted in thirty years.

That is the real cost of buying late. Early buyers sold into the enthusiasm and took their gains. Late buyers paid the highest prices, on the most extreme expectations, and then waited the longest, in some cases for decades, to see them justified. The burst is a single moment, but the people who bought last carry its cost for a generation.

## What to watch, and the one defense that matters

First, a caveat, stated once: none of this tells you when. Bubbles can run far longer than seems reasonable, and no signal here is a timing tool.

What you can do is run a concrete check instead of relying on a feeling. Look at how much of the buying is financed by borrowing. This ties directly back to the debt section, and it is the sign that predicts severity. A bubble funded by cash is painful. A bubble funded by leverage is the kind that turns into a crisis.

Then apply the dot-com lesson. Ask whether the price has anything underneath it, meaning whether the asset produces something that justifies what people are paying, or whether the price depends only on someone else paying more later.

Then apply a personal test. Ask whether you could hold your position through a fall and a very long recovery without needing the money.

Of all the advice one could give, only the leverage advice is worth keeping, because it mirrors the mechanism that does the damage. Don't borrow to buy something whose price rests on expectation. Debt is what turns a falling price into a deadline.

That is the whole defense: don't be a forced seller. The spiral of default, lender retreat and forced selling runs on people who have no choice but to sell at the bottom. If you are not one of them, the burst can hurt your portfolio without taking your future, and that is the reason to hold the fund the way you do: so that you can wait.

Bubbles are some of the most volatile and most worrisome of financial phenomena. Yet they also capture the human fascination with extremes. It’s easy to see how they draw attention when asset prices rise rapidly and then collapse. It’s harder to understand their spread and severity, but understanding the risk factors can help investors weather them and avoid ruin.

The Bubble is a Uniquely Financial Phenomenon

The first step toward understanding the risks bubbles pose is to define what a bubble is. A bubble is when asset prices rise on the expectation of ever-rising prices, with little regard for underlying fundamentals. Think tulip bulbs in Holland in the 1600s, stocks in the US in the 1920s, tech stocks in the late 1990s, and housing in the mid-2000s. With bubbles, prices become detached from underlying value and reality.

Price is Driven by Expectation, Not Output

The most vivid part of bubbles is their rapid rise and collapse. The rise occurs because investors believe prices will rise, so they bid up asset prices, which in turn reinforces their belief. The fall occurs when this self-fulfilling expectation breaks down, often when the price becomes too high relative to some reference point, such as its historic price, or when the cost of carrying the asset becomes a problem. Because so much of a bubble’s rise is built on expectation, this mechanism can lead to overshooting—meaning prices fall below their intrinsic value. This is why it’s important to understand what drives bubble formation and collapse.

Leverage is the Multiplier

Debt is a crucial element of most bubbles’ formation and spread. Buying assets on margin, when an investor puts down only a fraction of the asset’s price and borrows the rest, increases both potential gains and losses. The more debt, the larger the impact on asset prices and the bigger the losses when prices fall. As debt fueling a bubble builds, some borrowers are forced to sell assets to pay their loans. These forced asset sales can depress prices, triggering more forced selling and further price declines. This is how leverage can act as a multiplier on asset prices—and risks—during a bubble’s formation and collapse.

A bubble’s reach can extend far beyond the asset class with the runaway prices, in part because of the financial system’s interconnectedness. For example, some holders of the asset may have to sell other assets to pay off loans on the bubbly asset, which in turn can depress prices on those other assets. The ensuing losses can trigger margin calls on those other assets, which lead to further forced selling. This is how a bubble can spread beyond its original asset class.

A Bubble Can Turn a Crash Into a Crisis

How much damage a bubble causes depends on how much leverage it fuels, how fast it grows and spreads, and how much the underlying asset is worth. Because these factors differ from bubble to bubble, their outcomes can vary. Some bubbles lead to a crash in the asset class alone, with minimal impact on the broader economy. Others lead to a crisis and broad economic fallout.

A bubble where prices rise rapidly and underlying fundamentals are weak can lead to a crash and panic in the asset class when prices collapse. The ensuing losses can hurt financial firms, which in turn may have to raise cash by selling other assets, which fuels further price declines. If the bubble has spread widely enough, these losses can trigger a full-blown financial crisis. That’s what happened in the US during the subprime housing bubble in the mid-2000s and the ensuing financial crisis. Housing prices were artificially inflated, and the decline in prices devastated asset values. That led to losses and solvency problems for financial firms, which were forced to sell other assets and raise cash. Fears of losses on their loans led lenders to freeze credit, which stifled economic activity and led to a global recession.

Recoveries Are Measured in Decades

Bubbles are unique among financial phenomena because their boom-and-bust cycles are measured in years, while recoveries take much longer. Research into other bubbles suggests that it can take decades to rebuild the wealth lost during bubbles and crashes. Research on the US stock market in the 1920s found that it didn’t regain its 1929 peak until 1954. Similarly, research on the Nikkei Stock Index in Japan found that it didn’t regain its 1989 peak until 2016. That’s not the only downside to bubbles: Some research finds that bubbles and crashes affect economic growth. For example, the collapse of the US housing bubble in the mid-2000s led to the global financial crisis, which in turn led to a deep and prolonged US recession.

What Makes Some Bubbles Worse Than Others

Not all bubbles are alike. The size, speed, and breadth of the bubble are key factors in determining how bad its collapse will be. Bubbles with more leverage will tend to be more severe, as will those that spread to other asset classes and sectors. Bubbles that are built on real fundamentals are less likely to overshoot on the way down, so their collapses are less severe than bubbles with no underlying fundamentals, like tulip bulbs. Bubbles with a contagion mechanism, like subprime mortgages that led to the financial crisis, also tend to be more severe.

The One Factor that Really Matters

The best strategy for dealing with bubbles is to try to avoid being a forced seller. Forced sellers must sell at whatever price they can get, which tends to be near the bottom of the market. Forced sellers don’t care about fundamentals. Instead, they care about avoiding default. That’s why bubbles tend to lead to overshooting, when prices fall below their intrinsic value. Avoiding forced selling means you can wait for asset prices to recover.

Research suggests that there are two good strategies for avoiding becoming a forced seller: hold high-quality assets and don’t overleverage. Some financial firms—particularly those that don’t take on much leverage—can recover from bubbles without government help. Other firms, particularly those that didn’t take on much leverage, need government help to survive. For investors, maintaining a high-quality portfolio and keeping debt low are good ways to avoid being a forced seller during a bubble’s collapse.

Bubbles: What Makes Some Burst Harder and Heal Slower
How long does it take for some bubbles to heal when they burst? And why do some bubbles burst harder than others? These are questions we will discuss in this issue.

But first, let’s explain what a bubble is. Simply put, it is an increase in asset prices that has no basis in any kind of fundamental valuation. In other words, bubble is a price-driven process and not an output-driven one. That is, the fundamental objective of producing a good or a service is forgotten, and the sole purpose becomes increasing the price.

Let us take the housing industry as an example. The primary objective of constructing housing is to provide people with housing. During the bubble, however, homebuilders only thought about increasing the price of their houses. It was no longer a matter of supply and demand, but only demand.

The housing market is unique in the sense that it is the buyer, not the seller, who determines the price. The seller puts the house on the market at a certain price and the buyer either accepts it or rejects it. This is the reason

## Debt turns a crash into a crisis

The current crisis can be traced back to cheap money flowing into assets. The asset markets would have recovered from the bubble eventually, but the credit crisis made the situation much worse, as debt started a spiral of defaults and forced selling.

The result was that the prices of risky assets fell much more than they would have in the absence of leverage, and the banks and insurance companies were hit particularly hard. In the last analysis, it was leverage that turned the crash into a crisis.

The most important difference, however, is that in the absence of leverage, the losses would have been distributed across a much larger segment of the population, including most importantly the shareholders, instead of being concentrated in a small segment of the financial sector, as was the case during the last crisis.

In the absence of leverage, the number of people that would have lost their jobs and their houses would have been much smaller, and the impact on the real economy much less.

Now, let’s go back to our original question: Why do some bubbles burst harder than others? And why do some bubbles take longer to heal?

The simple answer is that the severity of the bubble depends on what causes the bubble to burst, and what happens after the bubble bursts.

## Recovery is measured in decades

The dot-com bubble was caused by valuations with no fundamental basis, so that when the bubble burst, the size of the fall was relatively small. In the case of Japan, however, the whole economy was affected, and in the absence of fundamental adjustments, it took more than 30 years before the economy recovered the lost ground. This is because in the case of bubbles with no fundamental basis, the value that was destroyed was speculative value, and not real value, so it could be easily recreated.

This is not the case, however, when the bubble is caused by something else. In the case of the housing market, for example, the fall was much greater than that of the internet bubble, and the recovery has been much slower. This is because housing is a real asset, and the value that was destroyed was real value, and not speculative value. It will take much longer to recreate this real value than it will take to recreate the speculative value, as was the case in the 1990’s internet bubble.

The same is true of the bubbles that cause monetary and financial crises. When a bubble bursts, and when there are no fundamental adjustments, it might take decades for the economy to recover.

## What to watch, and the one defense that matters

What does this mean for your investments? First, it means that it is hard to predict the timing of the end of bubbles. This is why it is almost impossible to predict the timing of the end of the housing market bubble, or of any other bubble.

What you can do is check to see how much of the bubble’s growth has been caused by debt and how much by fundamental improvements. In other words, you can check to see how much of the increase in asset prices is caused by debt, rather than by real increases in value.

If you see that the debt has been growing much faster than the fundamental values, then you know that the bubble will burst hard when there is a shock to the system, or when the system runs out of fuel.

The only defense you have against the bursting of the bubble is to avoid being a forced seller. That means that you must not own any assets that are financed with debt, either directly or indirectly. This is because debt creates leverage, and leverage turns a crash into a crisis.

The same rule applies to your investment fund. Avoid any investment fund that uses leverage. If you follow this rule, then no matter how hard the bubble bursts, you will not be forced into a fire sale, and you will have time to adjust to the new reality. To do so, you must own assets that are not financed with debt and that are used productively, and you must own them directly, without using debt.

A financial bubble is the dramatic rise in the value of an asset, especially in stocks or real estate, to a price far beyond what the underlying value justifies. Prices climb because buyers anticipate even more climbing – not because of more earnings, income, or usefulness.
Eventually, buyers lose their confidence and prices fall rapidly. This sudden drop is called a “burst.”
5. Credit Bubbles
Credit bubbles can be especially dangerous because the use of debt magnifies your losses. If the prices of your assets fall, you won’t be able to repay your lenders, and your lenders will pull back, causing forced selling, which pushes prices even lower. Money will flow into assets, lifting prices and encouraging even more borrowing.
1. Market Bubbles
The damage from market bubbles is rarely contained. If your home values fall, as happened in 2007-2008, they can hurt everyone from the banks that lend to you to the builders and insurers, and drag the wider market down sharply. If a stock becomes directly tied to the bubble, it will often fall the hardest, but companies that aren’t directly related to the bubble can also be pulled lower as investors sell whatever they can.
5. Credit Bubbles
The defining example of a credit bubble is the 2008 financial crisis. Bank stocks collapsed, and credit froze, and the S&P 500 fell more than 50% between its peak in 2007 and March 2009 low.
3. Stock Market Bubbles
The classic example is the dot-com bubble of the late 1990’s when money poured into internet companies, many of which didn’t make a dime and sometimes didn’t even have a business plan. The Nasdaq peaked in March 2000, only to lose roughly three-quarters of its value over the next couple of years. The recovery can take years; it took the Nasdaq more than a decade to regain its 2000 peak.
4. Economic Bubbles
The classic case of an economic bubble is what happened in Japan in the late 1980’s when soaring stock and real estate prices made the country feel invincible. The prices of both crashed in the early 1990’s, leading to a stagnating economy for years. The Nikkei peak in end of 1989, and didn’t return to that level for more than 30 years.
3. Stock Market Bubbles
A bad idea for beginners is to buy near the top of a market when a story is popular.
Warning Signs to Watch For
Although no one can time a crash perfectly, bubbles can inflate longer than seems rational. And these patterns recur. If you see prices climbing far above the underlying value of what’s being sold, for example comparing valuations like price-to-earnings ratios to historical averages, this should raise a red flag that something is wrong. If credit is easy, if lenders are extending loans to almost anyone, if borrowing is heavy, and leverage is being used, this can also amplify a bubble. If profits are weak or nonexistent, you should be wary of valuations based on promises rather than results.
If the main reason people are buying is because they fear missing out, you should consider pausing.
How New Investors Can Protect Themselves
Avoid using leverage while you learn. Keep an emergency fund to avoid being forced to sell your assets if they fall in a downturn.

Prices continue to climb on the expectation that they will continue to rise, rather than on the expectation of more earnings, income or usefulness. The impact of financial bubbles is especially dangerous because debt magnifies losses. If prices fall, borrowers cannot repay their loans, lenders pull back from lending, and forced selling pushes prices lower. But money also flows into assets, lifting prices and encouraging more borrowing.
1. Market Bubbles
The impact of market bubbles is rarely contained. When home values fell during 2007 and 2008, banks, builders and insurers were hit, pulling the wider market down sharply. Stocks tied directly to the bubble often fall hardest, but even unrelated companies can be pulled lower as investors sell whatever they can.
5. Credit Bubbles
Defining example: The 2008 financial crisis, when bank stocks collapsed, credit froze and the S&P 500 fell more than 50% from its 2007 peak to its low in March 2009.
3. Stock Market Bubbles
The textbook example of a stock market bubble is the dot-com bubble of the late 1990s, when money poured into internet-related firms, many of which never had any profits, and sometimes barely had a business plan. The Nasdaq peaked in March 2000 and lost roughly three-quarters of its value over the next couple of years. Recoveries from these types of bubbles can take years, with the Nasdaq not regaining its 2000 peak until 2015.
4. Economic Bubbles
The classic case of an economic bubble is Japan in the late 1980s, when soaring stock and real estate prices made the country feel invincible, but both collapsed in the early 1990s, sending the economy into a state of stagnation that lasted for years. The Nikkei peaked at the end of 1989 and didn’t return to that level for more than 30 years.
3. Stock Market Bubbles
The danger for beginners is buying near the top of a bubble after a story becomes popular. No one can time a crash perfectly, and financial bubbles have a habit of inflating longer than seems rational, but patterns still tend to recur. When prices are far above underlying fundamentals – such as when valuations like price-to-earnings ratios are compared to historical averages and are found to be extremely high – it’s a sign that deserves skepticism.
When credit is easily available, with low lending standards, heavy borrowing and leverage, it can amplify the effects of a bubble.
When profits are weak or nonexistent, be wary of valuations that are based on promises rather than results.
If the main reason for buying a stock is that the price is rising, that’s a sign to pause.

# Gaucher Disease's Primed Brain Resists a Virus in Mice

Mice with a form of Gaucher disease that affects the brain fended off Sindbis virus better than expected. The likely reason is that the disease keeps their brains in a standing state of antiviral alert. The same chronic inflammation that usually counts as damage appears, in this test, to have protected them. The findings are preliminary. They come from mice, and nobody yet knows whether they hold for people with the disease or for those who carry a single copy of the faulty gene. The study raises the possibility that the disease's inflammation has a hidden upside.

## An alarm that never switches off

Gaucher disease is genetic. A cell's cleanup system fails, material builds up, and the cells come under strain. Only the neuronopathic forms, those that affect the brain, matter here.

In these forms, the brain shows signs of interferon activity even though no infection is present. The likely explanation is stress. The buildup in the cells appears to drive a chronic alarm that never shuts off, and interferon is the signal that keeps it going. Interferon is a signaling protein that puts cells on guard against viruses.

The usual view is that this kind of inflammation does harm. A brain that is constantly inflamed is generally assumed to be a brain under attack from its own defenses.

The study asked a different question. If the alarm is always on, does it leave the brain better prepared when a real virus arrives?

## The test

The researchers used Sindbis virus to see whether the primed alarm offers any real protection against infection.

The design was simple. Mice modeling neuronopathic Gaucher disease were infected with the virus, and their outcomes were compared with those of healthy mice.

The Gaucher mice resisted the virus better. The authors attribute this to the interferon response that was already running before the infection began.

The result has a bearing on treatment. Suppressing interferon might ease the chronic inflammation, but it would likely come at a cost: it could remove a defense that the brain is actively using.

## The carrier question

Carriers matter because the gene variant behind Gaucher disease is common, and the disease it causes is a real risk. Anything that keeps the variant in circulation is therefore of interest.

One way to explain that is the heterozygote-advantage idea: carrying a single copy of a harmful variant can bring a benefit even though carrying two brings disease. Sickle cell is the standard example.

The authors suggest that something similar may be at work here. Carriers might be better protected against certain viral infections, and that could help explain why the variant persists. They stop short of claiming it. They offer it as a possibility, not a conclusion.

The biggest gap is that the mice in this study modeled full disease, not the carrier state. Carriers have one faulty copy, not two, and there is no evidence that their brains show the same primed alarm. They may show a weaker version of it, or none at all. Until that is tested, the carrier idea rests on an inference from animals with a much more severe condition.

The second gap is that the study used one virus. Primed immunity might not help against others, and it could cut the other way. A brain already on alert might respond to some infections with too much inflammation, and that could cause harm instead of preventing it.

So the open question is whether carriers, with one copy of the variant and no disease, are actually better defended against viruses, or whether the protection seen here exists only in the brains of animals that are sick.

A new study reports that mice with a rare, life-shortening form of Gaucher disease had more neurons and better brains than mice without the disease when both groups were infected with a strain of Sindbis virus.

The researchers found that the brains of the mouse model for Gaucher disease produced a high level of interferon and succeeded in blocking viral replication. However, the same amount of interferon injected into the brains of normal mice had no effect against the virus.

The discovery, which the researchers said could help explain why people who have the genetic disease are more susceptible to certain types of infection, appeared in the Journal of Virology [2015;89(8):4668–4677] this week.

Gaucher disease is caused by mutations in the gene for the enzyme glucocerebrosidase, which breaks down a fatty substance called glucocerebroside. Genes for a number of other potentially fatal genetic diseases, including Huntington's disease and Parkinson's disease, can also lead to an accumulation of glucocerebroside. However, Gaucher disease is the only one that produces severe symptoms, which can include pain, bone fractures, hepatosplenomegaly, and the formation of tumors and cysts in the spleen and liver. Another feature of the disease is a disruption of the blood-brain barrier, which allows leukocytes to enter the brain.

The enzyme deficiency caused by Gaucher disease also primes the brains of mice with the disease to produce a high level of interferon in response to infection with Sindbis virus, which is closely related to the viruses that cause West Nile disease and Dengue fever. Sindbis virus was used in the study because the mouse model for Gaucher disease can survive an infection with it, whereas other types of viruses would kill the mice before researchers could study the effect of the disease on the virus.

The researchers found that the interferon produced by the brains of the mice with Gaucher disease bound to receptors on the surface of nearby microglial cells, which release cytokines that block viral replication. While the normal mice produced the same amount of interferon, they did not have any receptors on their microglial cells to which the interferon could bind.

Mice with Gaucher disease had fewer signs of inflammation in the spleen, a lower concentration of the virus in their brains, and better cognitive performance than mice that were not infected with the virus.

The researchers found that when they injected interferon into the brains of normal mice, it had no effect on their ability to fight the virus. They concluded that the microglial cells of mice with Gaucher disease are primed to respond to interferon, which is not the case with normal mice. They said that blocking interferon production with drugs might enable the brains of mice with Gaucher disease to fight off Sindbis virus, but that the trade-off would be a decrease in their ability to fight other types of infections.

The researchers said more research is needed to determine whether the effect they observed in the brains of mice with Gaucher disease holds true for the brains of human beings who carry the gene mutations that cause the disease.

According to the researchers, another question that needs to be answered is whether the brains of Gaucher disease patients produce interferon only in response to Sindbis virus, or whether they also produce it in response to other types of viruses.

The researchers said that answering these questions could lead to the development of therapies that will prevent the brains of Gaucher disease patients from producing interferon, and thereby enable them to fight off viral infections more effectively.

They added that although most people who carry the gene for Gaucher disease remain asymptomatic, their brains produce less of the enzyme that breaks down glucocerebroside, which could make them more susceptible to viral infection. The researchers said that their findings indicate that gene therapy could be effective in treating this condition.

The researchers said that the findings of their study will also be helpful in understanding the role of glucocerebrosides in neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson's disease.

The brains of mice with neuronopathic Gaucher disease, which destroys the nervous system and kills children, resist a virus better than healthy brains, according to new research. The findings are preliminary but suggest that Gaucher disease patients may be at lower risk of some viral infections than other people are, the authors write in The Fold. They propose that the protective effect is based on a neuronopathy-associated immune response that is primed to attack viruses because of ongoing mutations in neurons, the main cells of the brain.

## An alarm that never switches off

The primary cause of the neuronopathic form is a lifelong accumulation of fatty waste material called glucosylceramide (Glucose) in the cells of the brain, which damages and eventually kills cells called neurons. In Gaucher disease, this accumulation is due to a genetic mutation in the gene that encodes the enzyme glucocerebrosidase (Glucose) that breaks down glucosylceramide.
The resulting accumulation of glucosylceramide in the brain, which causes GBA neurons to activate the interferon signaling pathway, which is a normal, antiviral defense. The team previously found that this signaling is constant in neurons with GBA mutations and that it is unable to return to its normal resting state. They predicted that this continuous activation may protect the brain from infection, and they tested this idea in the current study.

## The test

The researchers tested the ability of the brains of mice with the neuronopathic form of Gaucher disease to resist a virus called Sindbis virus. In these mice, the researchers found that the virus grew more slowly and that the mice had lower levels of viral replication in their brains than healthy mice did. Because the interferon response was primed in the brains of the Gaucher mice, the researchers attributed their resistance to this primed state.
The team also found that 1-month-old mice with the neuronopathic form of Gaucher disease had higher levels of proteins that are involved in an antiviral response than did the brains of age-matched healthy mice. Based on these findings, the researchers suggest that in humans, patients with the neuronopathic form of Gaucher disease may be less likely to develop some viral infections than are other people.
The team noted that their findings do not mean that Gaucher disease patients should stop receiving treatment, however. The current treatment is a drug that suppresses the interferon response. The authors’ findings suggest that this suppression has a price, but there is no reason to stop the treatment until new studies establish whether their results hold true in humans.

## The carrier question

The authors also noted that the mutation that causes Gaucher disease is common in the human population, which suggests that the neuronopathic form of the disease has persisted despite its lethality. This observation led the authors to speculate that carriers of the mutation might be at lower risk of some viral infections than are other people. In this scenario, having one copy of the mutation might protect carriers from infection without making them sick.
This idea is similar to that of heterozygote-advantage, which posits that carriers of a disease-causing mutation might have an advantage over other people in some situations. For example, carriers of the mutation that causes sickle cell disease may have resistance to malaria. The authors suggest that a carrier advantage would be consistent with their mouse findings, but they recognize that there is currently no evidence to support this idea in humans.
The authors propose that the sickle cell analogy may hold true for Gaucher disease, which would imply that carriers of the mutation might have lower infection rates than other people, but they caution that this suggestion is speculative and not evidence-based.
Gaucher mice
The authors note that their mouse study is not directly comparable to human disease. Their mice had a full-blown neuronopathic disease, but it is unknown whether carriers of the mutation would have a similar priming of the interferon response. The authors also point out that the Sindbis virus is only one of many different viruses, and the priming effect could have a different outcome with another virus.

In the disease Gaucher disease, the brain's immune response appears to make mouse brains more resistant to Sindbis virus – though those results are preliminary and we're not talking about people yet.
In people with neuronopathic Gaucher disease, the immune response has a pathway that seems to switch on – without infection – causing a buildup of lipid inside cells and triggering a chronic, low-level alarm. Hundreds of genes are turned on by the switch, activating the nearby cells into an "antiviral state." Inflammation is typically thought to drive the damage to neuronal cells and the progression of the disease. But what happens in the brain when that antiviral response is primed by viral infection?
In mice, Sindbis virus infects neurons and causes encephalitis, making it a useful model for studying how the brain defends itself. When the authors compared mice that carry the traits of the disease in their brains with control mice that were both exposed to the virus, they found that protection was linked to a pre-existing type I interferon response and the ongoing activation of the immune system provided a head start.
However, the double-edged sword of inflammation can be tricky. While neuroinflammation is often treated as a problem that needs to be suppressed, the same processes can also be protective. If future therapies target the interferon pathway in Gaucher disease, it's important to consider both sides.
Gaucher disease variants are a significant genetic risk factor for Parkinson's disease, and some populations have elevated carrier rates, including Ashkenazi Jews. So why do some disease variants persist in the population? The classic explanation is that carrying one copy of an allele might provide a disease-associated advantage. Sighted cell trait and malaria protection are the best-known examples, but we need to consider whether patients with Gaucher disease and possibly GBA carriers have some protection against certain viral infections. This is an important question to consider but not a conclusion.
As our models for disease better resemble patients, it's important to continue to test in human cells and patient populations, as well as carriers.

# Marriage Has Always Been Redefined

We are told that marriage is one fixed thing: one man, one woman, passed down unchanged from the beginning, and that any change to it is a break with the past. That story is a myth. Marriage has been defined and redefined by every society that has practiced it, and the version many people call traditional is only one stage in a long sequence of revisions. The question is not whether marriage may change, because it always has. The question is which definition we now live under, and what follows from it.

## Rome: a bargain

In Rome, no priest was required. Consent and intent were enough to make a marriage. The legal core was *affectio maritalis*, the continuing intention of two people to be married to each other. The law did not ask for a ceremony as proof of the bond. It asked whether the couple meant it.

Divorce followed from the same logic. If consent created a marriage, then withdrawn consent could end it. The arrangement held only as long as the intention did.

Love was optional. A marriage could be affectionate, but the law did not require it and did not measure it. Hold onto that detail, because it sets up a later inversion.

The takeaway is simple: in Rome, marriage was a bargain between two consenting parties, not a status conferred by an institution.

## The Church fixes the definition

The next great redefinition came when the Church made marriage a sacrament, a development of the 12th and 13th centuries. The year 1215 is a useful anchor. By then, marriage was no longer simply a matter of private consent. It belonged to the Church.

This is where "one man, one woman, for life" hardens into the form we now call traditional. Consent and intent no longer stood alone as the core of marriage. The union was defined as a sacred and permanent bond, and the definition was fixed accordingly.

It then proved durable. It survived the Reformation, and the states that later emerged inherited it. The definition passed from the Church to the state largely intact, even as the authority behind it changed.

## Love becomes the point

Once the state took over the administration of marriage, the institution began to change again. Marriage became a legal matter, handled by civil authority rather than religious authority.

Then came the inversion of Rome. Romans treated love as optional; we treat it as the point. Marriage is now understood as a union of two people who choose each other because they love each other. Consent still matters, as it did in Rome, but the purpose has been reversed.

This is the pivot of the story, and it explains why the modern question follows. If marriage rests on love and consent between two people, then it is fair to ask why the law should care about anything else.

## Tradition's best case

The best case for tradition begins with caution. Old institutions carry knowledge that is easy to lose, and changing them carelessly can do harm. That caution is reasonable. But history undercuts it here, because the institution being defended has been changed many times.

The strongest substantive claim is procreative: marriage exists to bind together the people who create children and to give those children stability. Stated fairly, it is a serious argument about what marriage is for.

But the answer is direct. We already marry people who cannot have children, or who choose not to, and we do not treat their marriages as lesser. The model we live by rests on consent and commitment, not on procreation.

The religious claim is that marriage belongs to God's design. It deserves one line in reply: the state took over marriage, and civil marriage answers to civil law.

## Where that leaves us

The law attaches real rights and obligations to marriage, so who may marry is not a symbolic question.

Under the model we already live by, which is consent between two people who choose each other, the gender of the couple is irrelevant. It plays no part in what the law asks. Marriage has moved from Roman bargain to sacrament to civil union of love, and at each step it was redefined. The next step does not break with that history. It follows from it.

That’s really the only throat-clearing needed to state the thesis: marriage has always been whatever society defined it to be. From first to last, marriage has been a legal institution, not a religious or philosophical one. Roman law gave us the enduring legal core of affectio maritalis, an agreement between two people to live together as man and wife – the logic of consent followed, in a society that honored few universal principles, from the right to divorce. The motives, or the intention, were legally irrelevant. Marriage wasn’t about love – it was about property, inheritance, legitimacy. Consent was all that mattered, and love was merely optional.
This Roman approach survived the Christianization of Europe, and when the Church eventually defined marriage as one of its seven sacraments, the Roman definition remained intact. The 12th and 13th centuries saw a flourishing of Christian theology, but it’s only in 1215 that we see the Church hardening the definition of marriage, decreeing that all marriages must take place in a church, be performed by a priest, and be witnessed by the community. It was the first step toward establishing marriage as a sacrament. But the Church had to keep its definition of marriage tight, because it was a definition shared by states. The European states inherited it, codified it, and kept it.
Fast-forward through the Reformation, and then the nation-state, and the Church had lost much of its authority over marriage. By the 1700s, the state had taken over the administration of marriage, granting licenses and tracking the legal obligations of marriage, and marriage had become a secular institution with a legal status.
In this context, the modern question of gay marriage follows inexorably. The state’s definition of marriage has always been flexible, always subject to change. The religious argument for marriage had been defeated, and the historic definition had been subject to dramatic revision. The state’s administration of marriage made it a secular institution, subject to the courts and to social change. And the question was no longer about love, but about the secular nature of marriage. The marriage we have now was a product of the state’s administration and the state’s definition, regardless of the procreative arguments that are now being deployed – arguments that we’ve heard before. The state’s administration of marriage has always been the real definition of marriage.

Marriage Has Always Been Redefined
The "redefinition of marriage" has become an increasingly popular rallying cry for opponents of marriage equality. But same-sex marriage is no more the "redefinition" of marriage than interracial marriage is. Marriage has always been redefined.
The concept of "one woman and one man" has not been consistent throughout our history, and the rights of marriage have continually evolved. Just a few centuries ago, marriage wasn't even about love-it was a way of binding together two families that had amassed some wealth and power, and passing on that power through the male heir. If love entered the picture at all, it was after the marriage was arranged.
Throughout history, women were property; they had few rights and only gained them slowly over time. In fact, it wasn't until the 16th century that women were even allowed to own property in their own name. A common misconception is that women couldn't vote at one time,

## Rome: a bargain

In fact, women have always had the legal right to marry, because that right could be easily traced back to its origins. Under Roman law, the only requirement for a valid marriage was the "affectio maritalis," which was a mutual consent between a man and a woman to become husband and wife. The presence of a priest, or any witnesses, were not required. Such a marriage had to be consummated, however, so it was valid only if the couple had sex.
Affectio maritalis was the legal core of marriage. Even after the Church made marriage a sacrament around the 5th century, it did not have the power to declare a couple married unless they had the affectio maritalis. If two people wanted to get married, but were afraid to do it publicly, the Church could recognize their marriage in secret if they met the basic requirements. In this way, the Church gained authority over all marriages, even those that happened without its involvement.

## The Church fixes the definition

The Roman church first established marriage as a sacrament in the 12th or 13th century. The church wanted to maintain control over who could get married, and who could get divorced. It was at this time that the church began its relentless attempts to define marriage in terms of "one man, one woman, for life." By 1215, the church hardened its position, requiring that all marriages must have witnesses, which made it much more difficult to have secret marriages.

## Love becomes the point

By the 16th century, after the Protestant Reformation, the church had even less power over marriage. The Roman Church continued to fight against its erosion of control over marriage, but it had been essentially reduced to a sacrament of the state, and not the church. As late as 1603, the church attempted to strengthen its control over marriage with the Council of Iguacu, which declared that "marriage is first and foremost a legal contract, rather than a sacred bond." This decree was in response to the growing secular concept that marriage was about love, and not just property.
In his book, Marriage, AHistory, the historian Lawerencestone makes the point that the church was strongly opposed to the concept of marriage for love, which was thought to weaken the bonds of marriage. But this idea was being promoted by poets and playwrights, who were beginning to challenge the church's complete control of marriage. Shakespeare's play, "AMidsummerNight'sDream," even ends with a marriage driven by love and not arranged by the parents. Of course, love was still not the focus of marriage in the 16th century, but the seeds were being sown for the concept that marriage was more than a legal contract between two families.

## Tradition's best case

Today, proponents of traditional marriage still argue that marriage is "between one man and one woman," and that it is a historical fact. But a cursory glance at the history of marriage shows that marriage has always been an evolving institution. In fact, the only constant in marriage is that it has always been changing.
The argument that marriage has "always" been between one man and one woman is also undercut by the fact that advocates for "traditional marriage" also believe that marriage is "about procreation." There have been countless same-sex marriages throughout history, as the scholar, stephanie coontz, has shown in her extensive research. And if marriage isn't about love, then it is solely about procreation, which is only true if the state is involved. Otherwise, two unmarried people who have children together can't form a family, which is ridiculous. The claim that "marriage is about procreation" is simply a political claim, and not a fact.

The question of marriage
Today, a marriage that is driven by love is the norm. While people in modern marriages often have children, many don't, but few people are trying to annul those marriages simply because they don't produce children. The fact that some people can't have children, or choose not to, is never grounds for annulment. The state recognizes this fact, and so should the church.
The states in our union have the authority to declare who is married, and it is only in the modern era that the states are ceding that authority to the

## Where that leaves us

Churches can still declare marriages, and in some instances, even annul them, but their authority over marriage is strictly limited. The state has the final say in all marriages. The question of who gets to marry is a legal question, and the legal answer is that gender is simply not relevant. Therefore, bans on same-sex marriage are both unconstitutional and immoral.

Marriage is widely believed to be a timeless, fixed institution - a universal practice sanctified by God as a union between one man and one woman. In fact, marriage has always been redefined in terms of who can marry, and how many people are involved.

During the Roman empire, for example, marriage was seen as a civil affair of public concern, and the state had the power to regulate it. The Christianity of the state emperor of Rome (Constant mine) in 100 a.d. shaped marriage as we know it today, and for centuries, it was accepted that marriage was a union between two people of the opposite sex.

## Rome: a bargain

In the Roman empire, marriage was a bargain between parties; no priest was needed. Consent and intent were enough to marry, and the legal core of a marriage was called a “affectio maritalis”. Divorce followed from the logic of consent: end the consent, and you end the marriage. Love was optional, and marriage was defined by agreement, not by love or ceremony. If a man died, the widow could marry his brother to keep the estate in the family. A widower could marry his brother’s widow for the same reason; she was just a part of the property, along with the house. Our modern concept of divorce, “til death do us part”, comes from the idea that a marriage ended when one spouse died.

## The Church fixes the definition

The Church began to claim dominion over marriage with the 12 th century. It was declared a sacrament, by which two became one in the eyes of God. In 1215, the Church decreed that all marriages must take place in church, and banned marriage between children, and marriages to close relatives. And that is where the definition of one man, one woman, for life came from, even though polygamy was still legal in some states, as late as 160. The definition survived the Reformation, and the states inherited it, with the concept of marriage as a legal contract, rather than a sacrament.

Author: Sue Sacrament

## Love becomes the point

The state took over administration of marriage in the 160 th century, and the concept of marriage became more a commitment based on love, rather than property or political alliances. This is the pivot, and why the modern question of same-sex marriage follows. If love is the point of marriage, then why not two people who love each other? This is not about changing marriage, but recognizing the change that has already taken place.

Author: Sue Sacrament
In an attempt to protect its interests, as the state took over more of marriage administration, the Church created civil marriage, which had no religious connotations. In the 160 th century, marriage became primarily about love, and without the Church, love became the only requirement. Once the religious or spiritual element was removed from the equation, all that was left was the state’s legal recognition of marriage, and as the state’s definition of marriage became more focused on property and inheritance, so did the Church’s definition.

## Tradition's best case

Marriage traditionally has been between a man and a woman, because it is the only combination that can produce children. This is the procreative claim.

Marriage is, and always has been, primarily about property and inheritance rights. Love is not a requirement, and it wasn’t until the 160 th century that the idea of marriage based on love was born.

The idea that marriage is a religious institution is challenged by the existence of civil marriage. Civil marriage is a purely legal contract that does not require any spiritual or religious element.

The answer to the procreation claim
The answer to the procreation claim is that same-sex couples can raise children, there have been same-sex couples throughout history, same-sex couples adopt, same-sex couples have intimate relations, and same-sex couples can form lifelong emotional bonds.

Religion has no claim to marriage, because the state is the sole administrator. When people get married, they get a marriage license from the state, not the church. The state is part of marriage, the Church is not.

## Where that leaves us

Where that leaves us is here: the state has jurisdiction over marriage and has created a model of marriage as a legal contract between two people. Gender is irrelevant under this model.

The state can change who is allowed to marry, because the state does not have to answer to any moral authority, religious or otherwise. The state issues marriage licenses, not the Church.

The defenders of “the traditional definition” of marriage, imagine their one stable arrangement handed down from the past, but that historical record is messier.
Marriage as a Practical Bargain
Marriage doesn’t need a priest or a religious ceremony. The affectio maritalis is consent and the intention to live together as husband and wife.
Divorce was comparatively easy, because it rested on consent rather than a sacred bond and ended when consent ended. Romance was not expected to be a foundation, but affection could grow. Love was a pleasant bonus, not a requirement.
The point is that marriage was never primarily about romantic fulfillment. Marriage was an economic and political technology.
The Church Takes the Wheel
Marriage was formally one of the seven sacraments in the 12 th and 13 th centuries. The Fourth Lateran Council in 1215 tightened the rules, including public announcements of intended marriages, in order to curb secret unions and clarify who had been wed.
Divorce became much harder, because the union between one man and one woman was now fixed in Western law and culture. After the Reformation, Protestants did not accept the marriage as a sacrament, but still saw it as a divinely ordained institution. Civil governments inherited the definitions of marriage created by the Church.
From Sacrament to Civil Right
The modern era loosened the grip of the Church. Civil marriage statutes and secular courts, no-fault divorce transformed marriage into a legal status run by the state. Society shifted its focus from marrying for material gain to marrying for love. What was once considered a side benefit of marriage became the central justification.
The crucial point here is that the current debate over marriage is the result of the basic question what does marriage mean? If marriage is defined as a loving and committed partnership between two adults, then limiting it to opposite-sex couples becomes a pressing question.
The Case for the Traditional Definition
I think the most respectable argument for the traditional definition is caution. Marriage is already a redefined institution, as the end of arranged marriages and no-fault divorce illustrate. The procreative argument is that marriage unites the two kinds of people who can create children, thereby giving children a mother and father.
The Case for Equality and Love
Child-less or infertile couples marry, without their legitimacy being questioned.
The Case for the Traditional Definition
Religious arguments include that marriage is a sacred institution, and that it is defined by faith. Changing marriage alters something that is never the state’s to change.
The Case for Equality and Love
Advocates of same-sex marriage point out that the state awards certain benefits, such as inheritance, hospital visitation, tax treatment, parental rights, and immigration status, to married people. Denial of these benefits to some couples is unequal treatment. Marriage is a civil right.
The Love-Based Marriage
Most people already operate with a love-based marriage model. If marriage is about two adults marrying for love and a shared life together, the gender of the partners is irrelevant to the modern purpose of marriage.
A society that celebrates marriage for love cannot justify excluding people who love differently.

Defenders of the “traditional definition” of marriage imagine that marriage has always been a single, stable arrangement handed down unchanged over time. The historical record is a bit messier. For one thing, no priest or religious ceremony was needed for a marriage; all that was necessary was the consent of the parties and their intention to live as husband and wife (the affectio maritalis). Divorce was comparatively easy because the marriage rested on the continuing consent of the parties rather than on a sacred bond that could not be broken. Romantic fulfillment was not expected as the foundation of marriage, although affection could grow; love was a pleasant bonus, not a requirement.
The point is that the institution was never primarily about the romantic fulfillment of the individuals involved. For most of history, marriage was an economic and political technology.
By the 12th and 13th centuries, marriage had been formally declared one of the seven sacraments. The Fourth Lateran Council, in 1215, tightened the rules, requiring, among other things, that intended marriages be announced publicly and prohibiting secret unions in order to clarify who was, in fact, wed. Divorce became far harder, since marriage was now understood as a lifelong union of one man and one woman, a union that was fixed in Western law and culture. After the Reformation, Protestants rejected the sacramental notion of marriage but still saw it as a divinely ordained institution. Civil governments, in turn, inherited the definitions set by the Church.
In the modern era, the Church’s grip on marriage was loosened by the introduction of civil marriage statutes, secular courts, and no-fault divorce. The idea of marriage as a legal status to be run by the state was strengthened, and the culture shifted toward marrying for love. What had been a side benefit of marriage became its central justification. It is crucial to the current debate that, if marriage is understood as a loving and committed partnership between two adults, then the question of whether to limit this institution to opposite-sex couples becomes a pressing one.
I find the caution argument the most respectable of the arguments for the traditional definition of marriage. But, I must admit, that argument has been weakened by the fact that marriage has been repeatedly redefined in the past (for example, the end of arranged unions and the advent of no-fault divorce). The procreative argument is that marriage unites the two kinds of people who can create children, and marriage provides those children with a mother and a father. But childless and infertile couples are never questioned about the legitimacy of their marriages.
The religious argument is that marriage is sacred, and its definition is determined by faith. Changing that definition therefore changes something that was never the state’s to change.
Advocates of same-sex marriage point out that the state gives legal benefits to married couples, including inheritance rights, hospital visitation, tax treatment, parental rights, and immigration status. Denying some couples these benefits is unequal treatment; marriage is a civil right. They also argue that the most common model of marriage that people already hold is based on love. If adults are free to marry for love and to live their lives together, then the gender of the partners is irrelevant to the modern purpose of marriage. Indeed, for a society that celebrates marriage for love, it is difficult to justify excluding people who love differently.

Defenders of the traditional definition of marriage imagine a single, stable, and unchanging arrangement passed down from generation to generation. But the historical record is a little messier.
Marriage could exist without either a priest or a religious ceremony. It required the consent of the parties and their intention to live as husband and wife (the affectio maritalis), but not any particular ritual or sacrament. Divorce was comparatively easy, because marriage rested on the continuing consent of the parties, not on a sacred bond, and it ended when that consent ended. Romantic love was not expected to be a foundation of marriage; affection could grow, but love was a pleasant bonus, not a requirement.
The point is that the institution was never primarily about romantic fulfillment. For most of history, it was an economic and political technology.
In the 12th and 13th centuries, marriage was formally recognized as one of seven sacraments. In the Fourth Lateran Council of 1215, the rules were tightened, including a requirement for a public announcement of intended marriages in order to discourage secret unions and clarify who was married. Divorce became far harder, and marriage was fixed in Western law and culture as a lifelong union between one man and one woman. After the Reformation, Protestants rejected the sacramental nature of marriage but continued to see it as a divinely ordained institution, and civil governments inherited the Church’s definitions.
In the modern era, the Church’s grip on marriage began to loosen, as civil marriage statutes, secular courts, and no-fault divorce allowed marriage to be recast as a legal status run by the state. As the culture shifted to the idea that people should marry for love, the former side benefit of marriage became its central justification. This is crucial to the current debate: If marriage is defined as a loving, committed partnership between two adults, then limiting marriage to opposite-sex couples becomes a pressing question.
I find the caution argument to be the most respectable of the defenses of the traditional definition of marriage, but it is weakened by the fact that marriage has already been redefined repeatedly (by the end of arranged unions and no-fault divorce, for example). The procreative argument is that marriage unites the two kinds of people who can create children, and that it gives children a mother and a father. Of course, childless and infertile couples are permitted to marry without the legitimacy of their unions being questioned.
Finally, there is a religious argument that marriage is sacred, and that it is defined by a particular faith. To change it is to alter something that was never the state’s to change.
Those who favor allowing same-sex couples to marry cite the legal benefits that the state gives to married couples, such as inheritance rights, hospital visitation rights, tax treatment, parental rights, and immigration status. Denying some couples those benefits is unequal treatment, they argue, and marriage is a civil right. Most people already hold a love-based model of marriage: if adults marry for love and to share their lives, then the gender of their partners is irrelevant to the modern purpose of marriage. A society that celebrates marriage for love can hardly justify excluding people who love differently.
